title: Female Athletes Are Half as Likely to Return to High-Risk Sports Compared With Male Athletes After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: An Exploration of Return-to-Sport Outcomes Between Sexes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Differences in female and male athletes' return-to-sport (RTS) outcomes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) are not well understood. The purpose of this study was to explore sex-based differences in RTS rates and predictors of RTS after ACLR for athletes participating in high-risk sports.
HYPOTHESIS: Female athletes will have significantly lower RTS rates than male athletes.
STUDY DESIGN: Secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial comparing single-bundle hamstring tendon autograft ACLR with or without a lateral extra-articular tenodesis using the iliotibial band.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 1.
METHODS: Data from 500 patients who underwent ACLR and participated in high-risk (jumping, pivoting, cutting) sport before injury were included in the study. Three definitions of RTS were created: return to preinjury sport and level, return to any high-risk sport at any level, and return to any sport at any level. Return rates were reported for the overall sample, and separately for male and female athletes. Multivariable logistic regression models were constructed to investigate predictors of each RTS outcome.
RESULTS: Approximately 86.5% of patients returned to any sport, whereas 76.5% returned to a high-risk sport, and only 45.5% returned to their preinjury high-risk sport and level. Male athletes reported consistently higher RTS rates than female athletes. In the final model predicting return to high-risk sport, female athletes had 53% lower odds of returning to high-risk sports compared with male athletes (odds ratio [OR], 0.47; 95% CI, 0.29 to 0.76; P < 0.01). For female athletes, earlier surgical intervention, higher confidence in the knee, and a stable knee were significant predictors of returning to high-risk sport.
CONCLUSION: Female athletes are less likely to RTS after ACLR compared with their male counterparts; however, this discrepancy appears greatest for athletes returning to high-risk sports.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Female athletes in high-risk sports may be an important target population for interventions to improve RTS rates after ACLR, and psychological readiness and knee stability may be important treatment targets within this group.

title: Double-Bundle Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Provides Superior Short-to-Midterm Rotational Stability But Not Clinically Important Functional Gains Over Single-Bundle: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare the biomechanical and functional outcomes between single-bundle and double-bundle (DB) anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction techniques using the most current evidence, stratified by follow-up duration.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane databases were searched from 2013 to September 2025 for randomized controlled trials comparing single-bundle versus DB anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with a minimum follow-up of 24 months. Primary outcomes included anterior tibial translation, rotational stability (pivot shift), and patient-reported outcomes (subjective International Knee Documentation Committee, Lysholm score). Secondary outcomes included return-to-sport and graft failure rate. Continuous outcomes were pooled using inverse-variance random-effects models (DerSimonian-Laird) and dichotomous outcomes using Mantel-Haenszel fixed-effect models, with stratification by follow-up duration (24-48 months vs >48 months). Heterogeneity was assessed using the I 2 statistic.
RESULTS: Thirteen randomized controlled trials (1041 patients; 536 single-bundle, 505 DB; mean age 30.2 years; 68% men; follow-up 24-122 months) were included. At 24 to 48 months, DB reconstruction significantly reduced the risk of a positive pivot shift (risk ratio 0.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.43-0.84, P = .003; number needed to treat = 10) and showed statistically higher subjective International Knee Documentation Committee (mean difference 5.88 points, 95% CI 0.44-11.33) and Lysholm (mean difference 7.47 points, 95% CI 0.06-14.88) scores; however, neither reached established minimal clinically important difference thresholds (11.5 and 8.9 points, respectively). Anterior tibial translation did not differ significantly between techniques (mean difference -0.34 mm, 95% CI -1.04 to 0.35, P = .327). No study reported sex-disaggregated outcomes or individual-level minimal clinically important difference attainment. Beyond 48 months, no significant differences were observed for any outcome.
CONCLUSIONS: DB reconstruction shows statistically significant improvements in rotational stability and patient-reported functional scores at 24 to 48 months, but functional differences do not reach established minimal clinically important difference thresholds. No significant differences were observed beyond 48 months, a finding likely influenced by substantial study heterogeneity and graft selection. The current evidence does not support a universal clinical advantage for the DB technique; shared decision-making based on patient activity demands and surgeon experience remains essential.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

title: Sex-related differences after ACL reconstruction differ between early functional recovery and 5-year outcomes.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare early functional recovery and 5-year clinical, sports and psychological outcomes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) according to sex.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included consecutive patients who underwent primary ACLR between January 2017 and December 2019, with standardized 6-month functional and psychological assessment and available 5-year follow-up. Patients were analyzed according to sex. Baseline characteristics, 6-month quadriceps strength and hop-test performance, and 5-year patient-reported and sports outcomes were compared between groups. The primary outcome was recovery of preinjury activity level at 5 years, defined as a post-operative Tegner score greater than or equal to the preoperative Tegner score. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors independently associated with the primary outcome.
RESULTS: A total of 479 patients were included, comprising 173 women (36.1%) and 306 men (63.9%). At 6 months, men demonstrated higher quadriceps limb symmetry and lower hop-test deficits than women, whereas anterior cruciate ligament return to sport after injury (ACL-RSI) did not differ significantly between groups. At 5 years, overall return-to-sport rates were similar between sexes (187 [61.2%] men vs. 103 [59.5%] women, p = 0.85), but men had higher post-operative Tegner (6 [5-7] vs. 5 [4-7], p < 0.001), IKDC (82.5 [75.7-87.3] vs. 79.5 [72.8-86.3], p = 0.02) and ACL-RSI scores (77.5 [55.8-92.5] vs. 69.2 [53.3-85.8], p = 0.02) and were more likely to recover their preinjury activity level (137 [45.1%] vs. 48 [28.1%], p < 0.001). In the baseline-adjusted multivariable model, male sex was independently associated with recovery of preinjury activity level (odds ratio [OR] = 2.16, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.40-3.39; p < 0.001). This association persisted after inclusion of 6-month recovery variables (OR = 1.93, 95% CI = 1.20-3.15; p = 0.007), while lower single-hop deficit was also independently associated with the outcome.
CONCLUSIONS: Men and women did not demonstrate the same recovery profile after ACLR. Early differences were mainly functional, whereas 5-year differences involved recovery of preinjury activity level, subjective knee function and psychological readiness, despite similar overall return-to-sport rates. These findings suggest that return to sport should not be interpreted as equivalent recovery quality after ACLR.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Low graft failure after primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in professional soccer players: A retrospective cohort study of 232 knees from the SANTI Study Group.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study aimed to determine graft failure rates after primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) in professional soccer players and to evaluate factors associated with graft failure, including lateral extra-articular augmentation.
METHODS: A retrospective cohort study included 232 primary ACLRs in 215 professional soccer players: isolated ACLR (n = 31) and ACLR combined with a lateral extra-articular procedure (LEAP) (n = 201). The primary endpoint was graft failure, defined as symptomatic rupture confirmed clinically and by imaging or revision surgery. Time-to-event analyses accounted for variable follow-up. Contralateral ACL injury was recorded descriptively.
RESULTS: At a mean follow-up of 100 months, 13 graft failures occurred (5.6%). Unadjusted failure rates were lower in ACLR + LEAP versus isolated ACLR (4.5% vs. 12.9%), but survival analysis showed no significant difference (hazard ratio [HR] 2.48; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.49-9.87; p = 0.246). Multivariable Cox regression identified no independent predictors of graft failure. Mean time to graft failure was longer in the ACLR + LEAP group than in the isolated ACLR group (54.8 ± 52.0 vs. 36.6 ± 38.2 months). Reoperations occurred in 32 knees (17.7%), with rates of 15.2% in the ACLR + LEAP group and 30.0% in the isolated ACLR group (p = 0.0528). Increased preoperative laxity (≥7 mm; HR 2.72; 95% CI 1.23-6.17; p = 0.014) and bone-patellar tendon-bone graft use (HR 3.14; 95% CI 1.26-7.20; p = 0.037) were independent risk factors for reoperation. Contralateral ACL injury occurred in 27.1% of knees, more frequently in female athletes (48.7% vs. 22.8%). Among patients who experienced graft failure, 53.8% also had a contralateral ACL injury.
CONCLUSION: Primary ACL reconstruction in professional soccer players was associated with durable long-term graft survival. Although ACLR combined with an LEAP was associated with fewer graft failures than isolated ACLR, an independent protective effect was not confirmed. The high rate of contralateral ACL injury highlights the multifactorial nature of reinjury risk in this elite population.

title: Effects of blood flow restriction training in adult upper-limb musculoskeletal rehabilitation: A systematic review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Blood flow restriction training (BFRT) has been proposed as a low-load rehabilitation strategy for symptomatic and postoperative upper-limb musculoskeletal conditions. This review evaluated the clinical effects, tolerability, and prescription characteristics of BFRT in adult upper-limb musculoskeletal rehabilitation.
METHODS: This systematic review was registered in International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420261299726) and reported with reference to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020. CENTRAL/Cochrane Library, Embase via Ovid, MEDLINE/PubMed, Science Citation Index/Web of Science, and Scopus were searched without a start-date restriction before February 18, 2026; backward reference-list/citation checking was also used. Randomized trials, case series, and case reports were eligible. Findings were synthesized narratively because of heterogeneity, and studies were appraised using risk of bias 2 or design-appropriate Joanna Briggs Institute checklists.
RESULTS: Twenty reports were included: 9 parallel-group randomized trials, 1 randomized crossover trial, 2 case series, and 8 case-report publications. Across the reports, 340 participants were enrolled or randomized and 326 contributed to the analyzed/treated clinical samples; 158 were men (48.5%) and 168 were women (51.5%). In a sham-controlled lateral elbow tendinopathy trial, BFRT resulted in a significantly greater reduction in 12-week pain (between-group difference -1.54, 95% confidence interval [CI] -2.89 to -0.18; P = .026) and patient-rated tennis elbow evaluation (PRTEE) (-15.23, 95% CI -23.57 to -6.90; P < .001). In patients with chronic lateral epicondylitis, PRTEE reduction (-24.20 ± 4.02 vs -15.60 ± 3.71; P = .001) and quick disabilities of the arm, shoulder and hand reduction (-12.83 ± 4.97 vs -7.51 ± 4.72; P = .025) were significantly greater with BFRT plus conventional therapy, whereas between-group pain and strength changes were not significant. In nonoperative distal-radius-fracture rehabilitation, mean activity-pain reduction was 4.0 versus 2.3 points (P = .03). In rotator-cuff tendinopathy, BFRT resulted in significantly greater biceps thickness (P = .002) and internal-rotation strength (P = .040). Conversely, a pragmatic elbow trial found no significant between-group difference in 12-month PRTEE (adjusted contrast + 4.32, 95% CI -9.17 to 17.81; P = .53).
CONCLUSION: BFRT may be considered a low-load adjunct in adult upper-limb musculoskeletal rehabilitation settings, but it is not consistently superior to active rehabilitation for pain, strength, or function. Confidence remains limited by small samples, heterogeneous prescriptions and co-interventions, uncontrolled designs, and incomplete adverse-event ascertainment.

title: Clinical and functional predictors of delayed return to sport after first-time patellar dislocation in adolescents: A prospective cohort study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: First-time lateral patellar dislocation is common in adolescent athletes and may cause persistent functional impairment despite nonoperative treatment. Early predictors of delayed return to sport remain incompletely defined.
OBJECTIVE: To identify early clinical and functional factors associated with delayed return to unrestricted preinjury-level sport after first-time lateral patellar dislocation in adolescents.
METHODS: This prospective cohort study included 160 adolescents aged 12-18 years (97 females, 63 males) with first-time traumatic lateral patellar dislocation managed nonoperatively. Participants underwent standardized rehabilitation and were followed for 12 months. At 3 months, quadriceps limb-symmetry index (LSI), single-leg hop performance, Y-Balance asymmetry, patellar apprehension, Banff Patellofemoral Instability Instrument 2.0 (BPII 2.0), and Pediatric International Knee Documentation Committee scores were assessed. Delayed return to sport was defined as failure to resume unrestricted preinjury-level sport within 6 months. Associations were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression.
RESULTS: Seventy-six participants (47.5%) experienced delayed return to sport. Compared with timely returners, they had lower quadriceps LSI, poorer hop performance, greater Y-Balance asymmetry, more frequent patellar apprehension, and worse patient-reported function. Independent predictors were each 10-percentage-point decrease in quadriceps LSI (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.82, 95% CI 1.29-2.57), persistent patellar apprehension (aOR 2.71, 95% CI 1.31-5.62), and each 10-point decrease in BPII 2.0 score (aOR 1.51, 95% CI 1.13-2.02). The model showed good discrimination (AUC 0.80, 95% CI 0.73-0.86).
CONCLUSION: Reduced quadriceps symmetry, persistent apprehension, and poorer instability-specific function were independently associated with delayed return to sport, supporting multidimensional, criterion-based rehabilitation in adolescents.

title: Preoperative subacromial autologous conditioned plasma (ACP) injections and histological and immunohistochemical findings in degenerative supraspinatus tendon tears - results of a prospective comparative cohort study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Degenerative supraspinatus tendon quality is a key determinant of healing after rotator cuff repair, and advanced histological degeneration has been associated with increased retear rates. While platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been extensively studied as an intraoperative adjunct, the potential role of preoperative biological tissue conditioning using platelet-rich plasma remains poorly defined.
HYPOTHESIS/PURPOSE: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the association of preoperative subacromial PRP injections (autologous conditioned plasma, ACP®, Arthrex, Naples, Fl.) with histological and immunohistochemical characteristics of degenerative supraspinatus tendons at the time of rotator cuff repair. It was hypothesized that preoperative ACP treatment would be associated with lower Bonar and degeneration scores compared with untreated controls.
METHODS: A prospective comparative cohort study was performed including patients undergoing arthroscopic repair of isolated, degenerative full-thickness supraspinatus tendon tears. The intervention group received three preoperative subacromial ACP injections (two in one patient) within 3 to 4 weeks before surgery, with the final injection administered no more than 1 week preoperatively. A control group of patients who declined ACP did not receive biological preconditioning. Intraoperatively, tendon biopsies were harvested from the lateral edge of the supraspinatus tendon. The Bonar score and a semiquantitative degeneration score were the co-primary endpoints. Ki-67, CD31 and CD45/LCA immunostaining were exploratory endpoints.
RESULTS: Fifty-four patients were included (ACP group, n = 24, control group, n = 30). The ACP group had lower Bonar scores (6.5 ± 2.0 vs 8.2 ± 1.3, mean difference -1.7, 95% CI -2.7 to -0.7, adjusted P = .044) and lower degeneration scores (1.7 ± 0.8 vs 2.2 ± 0.6, mean difference -0.5, 95% CI -0.9 to -0.1, adjusted P = .044) than controls. CD31 immunostaining was higher in the ACP group, but this difference was not significant after correction for multiple testing (adjusted P = .100). Ki-67, CD45/LCA, reparative changes and the proportion of necrotic tissue did not differ between groups.
CONCLUSION: Preoperative subacromial ACP injections were associated with lower Bonar and degeneration scores in degenerative supraspinatus tendons at the time of rotator cuff repair. The differences were small, the difference in Bonar score was below the predefined minimal clinically important difference, and the clinical relevance of these findings is unclear.

title: The Use of Cupping (Hijama) Therapy Among Athletes and Its Relationship With Sleep Quality: A Cross-Sectional Study in Palestine.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Wet cupping, or Hijama, is commonly used by athletes for recovery, yet evidence regarding its relationship with sleep quality remains limited. This study examined cupping use, perceived benefits, adverse effects, and factors associated with self-reported sleep quality among Palestinian athletes.
METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among Palestinian athletes. Of 754 athletes screened at nine sports clubs and training centers across the West Bank, 470 (62.3%) reported previous wet-cupping use; 468 had sufficient primary-outcome data and were analyzed. Data were collected using a structured paper-based questionnaire incorporating the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Analyses included descriptive statistics, exact and chi-square tests, Spearman correlations, multiple linear regression, and path analysis.
RESULTS: Improved mobility (30.8%), reduced muscle cramps (25.6%), enhanced immunity (16.2%), and increased endurance (9.0%) were the most frequently reported intended benefits. Cupping was commonly reported for chronic or recurrent conditions (99.6%), muscle strain (41.5%), and headaches (41.2%). Higher BMI and greater cupping-session frequency were associated with greater perceived cupping benefit (p = 0.010 and p < 0.001, respectively). Reported inflammation was associated with BMI category, gender, and competition level, while mild pain was associated with BMI category and competition level. Lower PSQI scores were associated with higher BMI, greater cupping-session frequency, and greater perceived cupping benefit. In the multivariable model, higher BMI, vitamin use, greater cupping-session frequency, greater perceived benefit, and manual rather than automated suction were independently associated with lower PSQI scores. The model explained 35.2% of the variance in sleep quality.
CONCLUSION: Cupping-related practices and participant characteristics were associated with sleep quality. More frequent sessions, vitamin use, manual suction, higher BMI, and greater perceived benefit were associated with better sleep quality. These findings do not establish causality. Prospective studies are needed before cupping can be recommended to improve sleep or recovery.

title: Low Physical Therapy Referral Rates for Knee Osteoarthritis Present a Barrier to Care for Patients With Medicaid.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the rates of physical therapy (PT) referral for knee osteoarthritis (KOA) and factors associated with referral patterns, including insurance status, provider specialty, year, and patient demographics and comorbidities.
DESIGN: This retrospective cohort study included 41,373 patients diagnosed with KOA at an integrated health system in Arizona and Colorado, USA between January 2020 and February 2023. PT referral rates were stratified by insurance type. Multivariable logistic regression assessed predictors of referral including insurance type, age, BMI, sex, race/ethnicity, provider specialty, year of visit, and comorbidities.
RESULTS: Crude PT referral rates at the initial visit were 12.06% for Medicaid, 6.83% for Medicare, 10.29% for commercial insurance, and 8.33% for uninsured patients. Adjusted analysis showed that Medicaid patients had higher referral odds (OR, 1.20; 95% CI [1.10, 1.30]; p < 0.001), whereas Medicare patients had lower odds (OR, 0.76; 95% CI [0.66, 0.88]; p < 0.001) compared to those with commercial insurance. Female (OR, 1.21; 95% CI [1.14, 1.29]; p < 0.001) and Hispanic patients (OR 1.18; 95% CI [1.09, 1.29]; p < 0.001) demonstrated increased referral odds. Provider specialty was associated with PT referral, with non-operative sports medicine providers having the highest referral odds (OR, 3.00; 95% CI [2.72, 3.31]; p < 0.001) relative to orthopaedic surgery.
CONCLUSION: Despite strong clinical practice guidelines recommending PT, formal referral rates for patients with KOA remain low regardless of insurance type, patient characteristics, and referring healthcare provider specialty. Low formal PT referral rates may represent a barrier to evidence-based KOA care.

title: Field-Based Assessment of Running Biomechanics Using Global Positioning System/Inertial Measurement Unit: Establishing Construct Validity in Elite Athletes.
abstract: Weber, JA, Peeling, P, Hart, NH, and Newton, RU. Field-based assessment of running biomechanics using global positioning system/inertial measurement unit: Establishing construct validity in elite athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-To examine the between-session reliability and construct validity of global positioning system (GPS)/inertial measurement unit (IMU)-derived biomechanical variables during field-based running in elite athletes. Fifty-four professional male Australian Football League players completed repeated 40-m runs across 1 competitive season (3,943 trials). Running speed for the 20-40 m segment was quantified via 10-Hz GPS and center-of-mass displacement metrics derived from a 100-Hz IMU. Between-session reliability (n = 25, mean (k) = 2.95) was assessed using a linear mixed-effects model with velocity as a fixed covariate, expressed as intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) (absolute agreement), SEM, and minimal detectable change95, with 95% confidence intervals from athlete-cluster bootstrap. Five candidate models were compared; Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines was selected based on lowest cross-validation root mean squared error (RMSE). Validity was assessed over 100 iterations of athlete-stratified cross-validation (80/20 split), with agreement quantified by ICC, RMSE, and athlete-level Bland-Altman analysis. Velocity-adjusted reliability ranged from moderate to good-to-excellent across 12 variables (ICC = 0.65-0.92), with 8 meeting good-to-excellent thresholds (ICC ≥0.75). Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines accounted for 93% of variance in running speed (R2 = 0.93; RMSE = 0.20 m·s-1; ICC = 0.96 ± 0.004). Athlete-level Bland-Altman analysis indicated negligible bias (-0.01 m·s-1; LoA: -0.243 to +0.223 m·s-1) with no proportional bias (p = 0.369); limits narrowed in athletes with adequate data volume (n = 47; -0.207 to +0.189 m·s-1). Mechanics-speed relationships persisted after accounting for within-athlete clustering (residual between-athlete ICC = 0.43), and the most influential predictors were consistent with established biomechanical determinants of speed. These findings support GPS/IMU-derived biomechanical variables as field-based indicators of running mechanics. Pending replication and criterion validation, this approach may offer practitioners an accessible framework for monitoring performance and rehabilitation.

title: Reduced knee adduction moments in bicruciate-retaining total knee arthroplasty compared with bicruciate-substituting designs: A contralateral within-patient study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study compared frontal-plane knee loading during gait between bicruciate-retaining total knee arthroplasty (BCR-TKA) and bicruciate-substituting TKA (BCS-TKA) using a contralateral within-patient design.
METHODS: Twenty-five patients undergoing simultaneous bilateral TKA received BCR-TKA in one knee and BCS-TKA contralaterally. The final implant selection was determined intraoperatively based primarily on anterior cruciate ligament integrity and functional preservability. Postoperative radiographs were obtained within 1 week before gait analysis, performed 287.4 ± 160.6 days after surgery (range, 109-739 days). The primary outcome was the first peak knee adduction moment (KAM). Secondary outcomes were the second peak KAM and the KAM impulse. Linear mixed-effects models were adjusted for postoperative hip-knee-ankle angle (HKA), joint-line obliquity (JLO), and stance-phase knee varus angle.
RESULTS: Postoperative HKA (3.24 ± 3.1° vs. 3.50 ± 3.4°; P = 0.767) and JLO (178.33 ± 4.8° vs. 178.03 ± 5.0°; P = 0.757) were comparable between BCR-TKA and BCS-TKA. Adjusted first peak KAM was lower with BCR-TKA (BCS-BCR difference, 0.052 Nm/kg; 95% confidence interval, 0.011-0.094; P = 0.014), as was second peak KAM (difference, 0.035 Nm/kg; 95% confidence interval, 0.002-0.068; P = 0.038). KAM impulse did not differ significantly (P = 0.128). All patient-reported outcomes were comparable; Forgotten Joint Score-12 was 24.4 ± 10.7 vs. 25.6 ± 12.0 (P = 0.287).
CONCLUSION: BCR-TKA was associated with lower first and second peak KAMs despite similar postoperative alignment, whereas KAM impulse and patient-reported outcomes were comparable between the implant designs.

title: Retatrutide in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes (TRIUMPH-2): a double-blind, parallel-group, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Retatrutide is an agonist of GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon receptors, and is currently under investigation for the treatment of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other comorbidities, including knee osteoarthritis and obstructive sleep apnoea. We aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of retatrutide in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes.
METHODS: TRIUMPH-2 was a double-blind, parallel-group, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial conducted at 92 medical and research centres and hospitals across eight countries. We enrolled adults (aged ≥18 years) with a BMI of 27 kg/m2 or higher and type 2 diabetes (glycated haemoglobin [HbA1c] 6·5-10·5%) on stable treatment for type 2 diabetes for at least 90 days before screening (diet or exercise alone, or up to three oral glucose-lowering medications), and a history of at least one self-reported unsuccessful dietary effort to reduce bodyweight. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1), using an interactive web-response system, to receive once-weekly subcutaneous injections (self-administered) of placebo or retatrutide 4 mg, 9 mg, or 12 mg. The primary endpoint was the percentage change from baseline to week 80 in bodyweight for the retatrutide 9 mg and 12 mg doses versus placebo, with 4 mg versus placebo a key secondary endpoint. Efficacy analyses included all randomly assigned participants, with missing data imputed with a primary multiple imputation strategy for the treatment regimen estimand. Safety analyses included all randomly assigned participants who received at least one dose of study drug. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05929079 (completed).
FINDINGS: Between July 11, 2023, and Nov 1, 2024, 2047 participants were screened, and 1152 (mean age 55·1 years [SD 10·8], 554 [48%] females and 598 [52%] males, and 672 [58%] of White ethnicity) were randomly assigned to retatrutide 4 mg (n=292), 9 mg (n=284), or 12 mg (n=287), or placebo (n=289). At baseline, the mean BMI was 38·2 kg/m2 (SD 7·4), mean HbA1c was 7·71% (1·07), median duration of obesity was 21 years (IQR 11-31), and median duration of diabetes was 5·6 years (2·6-10·4). At baseline, 1055 (92%) of 1152 participants were on any oral glucose-lowering medication, including biguanides, SGLT2 inhibitors, sulfonylureas, and other oral glucose-lowering medications. Of 1152 participants, 965 (84%) completed the study drug. For the treatment regimen estimand, the mean percentage change from baseline in bodyweight at week 80 was -11·9% (SE 0·6) with retatrutide 4 mg, -16·8% (0·7) with retatrutide 9 mg, -18·8% (0·7) with retatrutide 12 mg, and -5·1% (0·7) with placebo. Estimated treatment differences compared with placebo for percentage change in bodyweight were -6·9% (95% CI -8·7 to -5·1) with retatrutide 4 mg, -11·8% (-13·7 to -9·8) with retatrutide 9 mg, and -13·8% (-15·8 to -11·8) with retatrutide 12 mg (p<0·0001 for all). The most frequently reported adverse events were gastrointestinal, which were more common in the retatrutide groups than in the placebo group (diarrhoea occurred in 80 [27%] of 292 participants in the 4 mg group, 95 [34%] of 284 in the 9 mg group, and 96 [34%] of 286 in the 12 mg group vs 38 [13%] of 287 in the placebo group, and nausea occurred in 40 [14%], 59 [21%], and 80 [28%] vs 23 [8%]). Hypotension and dysesthesia were more frequent with retatrutide than with placebo (four [1%] in the 4 mg group, 14 [5%] in the 9 mg group, and 18 (6%) in the 12 mg group vs one [<1%] in the placebo group with hypotension; 13 [4%], 16 [6%], and 21 [7%] vs two [1%] in the placebo group with dysesthesia). Permanent treatment discontinuation due to adverse events or death was more frequent in participants treated with retatrutide 9 mg (33 [12%]) and 12 mg (22 [8%]) compared with retatrutide 4 mg (11 [4%]) and placebo (14 [5%]). Two participants died in the retatrutide 4 mg group, three in the 9 mg group, one in the 12 mg group, and one in the placebo group; all deaths were deemed to be unrelated to the study intervention by the investigator.
INTERPRETATION: Treatment with retatrutide resulted in substantial improvements in bodyweight and was associated with improvements in glycaemic control in participants with obesity and type 2 diabetes, with a safety profile generally consistent with other molecules with GLP-1 receptor agonism. These results show that retatrutide might be effective for the treatment of obesity in people with type 2 diabetes.

title: Effects of acute Capsaicin analogue intake on athletic performance: a three-level meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Capsaicin analogues have been proposed as potential ergogenic aids, but their acute effects on athletic performance remain inconsistent. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of acute capsaicin analogue intake on exercise performance using a three-level meta-analysis.
METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, SPORTDiscus, and the Cochrane Library were searched up to April 1, 2025. Randomized controlled trials examining acute oral capsaicin analogue intake in healthy adults were included. Outcomes were classified into strength, power, muscular endurance, and aerobic capacity. Hedges' g was calculated using a three-level random-effects model.
RESULTS: Twenty-one randomized crossover trials with 67 effect sizes were included. Acute capsaicin analogue intake significantly improved overall athletic performance compared with placebo (g = 0.20, 95% CI [0.07, 0.33], p < 0.01). Subgroup analyses showed significant effects on power (g = 0.39) and muscular endurance (g = 0.25), but not on strength or aerobic capacity. Phenylcapsaicin showed the largest effect, and benefits were more evident in trained participants. Dose-response analysis suggested a nonlinear pattern, with low-to-moderate doses showing more stable benefits.
CONCLUSIONS: Acute capsaicin analogue intake may produce small but significant improvements in athletic performance, particularly in power and muscular endurance. However, due to heterogeneity, publication bias, and very low certainty of evidence, these findings should be interpreted cautiously.

title: Dietary Supplement Use and Beliefs Among Athletes at the 2025 Canada Games.
abstract: Dietary supplement use is widespread among athletes; however, limited data exist regarding supplement use and beliefs among Canadian youth athletes. This cross-sectional online study aimed to examine dietary supplement use and related beliefs among athletes competing at the 2025 Canada Games in St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador. A total of 473 respondents participated in the survey. Of the 473 participants, 385 completed responses to the dietary supplement (DS) questions. Among participants who reported their sex, 125 were male and 189 were female. Overall, 36% of participants reported current dietary supplement use. Supplement use was significantly higher among males than females (47% vs. 23%, p < .001) and increased with age (p = .001). The most commonly reported supplements were protein powder (49%), sports drinks (46%), and creatine (45%). Primary reasons for use included maintaining good health (76%), increasing energy (54%), and promoting recovery (50%). Coaches (50%) and healthcare professionals (49%) were the most frequently reported information sources. Supplement users demonstrated significantly stronger positive beliefs regarding benefits of dietary supplements compared with non-users (all p < .001). Ordinal logistic regression showed that supplement users had greater odds of stronger agreement that supplements improve performance (OR = 5.50, 95% CI: 3.31-9.13, p < .001). These findings highlight the use of dietary supplements among Canadian youth athletes and support the need for targeted nutrition education to promote informed decision-making.

title: Baseline Symptom Collection in Elite Rugby Union Players-Limited Clinical Utility? An Investigation of Assessments Across 5879 men and Women Athletes.
abstract: In World Rugby's Head Injury Assessment (HIA) protocol, a modified Sports Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT) is completed during the pre-season (baseline) and when a player has a suspected head injury. The symptom component of the SCAT, which involves comparing current to baseline symptoms, has been shown to be the most predictive component for concussion diagnosis. Because the clinical comparison of symptom report to baseline is a key determinant of concussion diagnosis, this study aims to explore the relationship between symptoms endorsement at baseline and during HIA. Mean and standard deviation (SD) or median and interquartile ranges (IQR) are presented along with relevant bivariate analyses. Logistic regressions compared proportions of symptom endorsement profiles between men and women. At baseline, 'Trouble sleeping' and 'Fatigue or low energy' were commonly reported symptoms for men and women. At baseline, women (mean + SD) reported more symptoms than men (mean + SD) on average. During the HIA, women players were nearly 3 times (Relative risk: 2.98 95% CIs: 2.47-3.60) more likely than men to report fewer symptoms immediately after the match than at baseline (47% women vs. 16% men). While this study highlights the importance of collecting baseline assessment as a medical overview of players, it de-emphasises the relevance of baseline symptoms when using the SCAT as a clinical assessment tool in professional rugby players. This study also highlights important differences in men and women's rugby players in symptom reporting, and recommends de-coupling baseline symptom reporting from the diagnostic part of the HIA.

title: Application of antibiotic-loaded bone cement in unicompartmental knee arthroplasty: inhibiting IL-6 levels and reducing postoperative infection rate.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: We aim to clarify the inhibitory effect of antibiotic-loaded bone cement (ALBC) on inflammatory factors, and its preventive effect on postoperative infections in unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA).
METHODS: This prospective randomized controlled trial enrolled 104 osteoarthritis patients undergoing UKA, randomly assigned to the non-ALBC group (n = 52, bone cement without antibiotics) and ALBC group (ALBC with 1.0 g vancomycin hydrochloride, n = 52). Primary outcomes were postoperative inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR, TNF-α, IL-6); secondary outcomes included infection rate and HSS score. Independent-samples t-tests were used for continuous variables, χ2 test for categorical variables (infection rate, efficacy), and repeated measures analysis of variance for intra-group longitudinal comparisons.
RESULTS: The ALBC group demonstrated lower inflammatory markers at postoperative day 7 and at 3 months [CRP (3.52 ± 0.81 vs 6.92 ± 1.17, Cohen's d = 3.379), ESR (16.29 ± 2.31 vs 20.19 ± 4.05, Cohen's d = 1.183), TNF-α (29.71 ± 4.03 vs 36.25 ± 5.17, Cohen's d = 1.411), and IL-6 (17.05 ± 3.72 vs 22.05 ± 4.38, Cohen's d = 1.230)] (all p < 0.001), and also showed superior clinical outcomes, with lower postoperative infection rate (p = 0.016), higher HSS score (p < 0.001), and better overall clinical efficacy (p = 0.010) than the non-ALBC group.
CONCLUSION: The application of ALBC in UKA was associated with reduced postoperative inflammatory markers such as IL-6 and a lower incidence of postoperative infection. These findings suggest that ALBC may play a beneficial role in postoperative recovery and joint function rehabilitation.

title: Shear wave elastography for assessing lower extremity muscle stiffness after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: A systematic review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) restores passive joint stability, yet athletes who meet strength benchmarks may still land stiffly, hesitate to push off, and re-injure. Muscle stiffness governs how rapidly force is transmitted to the joint, and shear wave elastography (SWE) quantifies it muscle by muscle, but SWE findings after ACLR have not been synthesized.
METHODS: Scopus, PubMed, SPORTDiscus, and CINAHL were searched through November 2025 following PRISMA 2020. Eligible studies compared SWE-derived lower-extremity muscle stiffness after ACLR with contralateral limbs or controls. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and appraised quality (Downs and Black). Findings were synthesized narratively with Hedges' g (95% confidence intervals) where data permitted.
FINDINGS: Six studies (173 ACLR participants, 79 controls; quality poor to good) were included. Reduced passive vastus medialis shear modulus was consistently observed in operative limbs (g - 1.10 to -1.21 versus controls) and was associated with quadriceps strength, knee function, and landing biomechanics. Semitendinosus stiffness was reduced after hamstring tendon harvest (g - 1.29 to -1.64) but not at mid-belly after return to sport. Longitudinal deficits persisted at three months; active-contraction findings conflicted. No study sampled the distal vastus medialis obliquus or the distal hamstring musculotendinous region.
INTERPRETATION: SWE detects muscle-specific mechanical deficits that relate to function beyond strength: a compliant vastus medialis offers a mechanical explanation for the strong patient who lands stiffly, and reduced semitendinosus stiffness marks donor-site morbidity. Standardized protocols that sample clinically relevant regions and follow patients to return to sport are needed before SWE can guide rehabilitation.

title: Pre-sleep milk-derived proteins do not impair sleep or recovery in elite female athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep is essential for athlete recovery and performance, yet athletes frequently experience restricted or poor-quality sleep. Pre-sleep feeding (PSF) has emerged as a strategy to support recovery, but randomized, double-blinded, crossover trials comparing PSF macronutrient options on objective and subjective sleep outcomes in elite female athletes remain limited.
METHODS: Twenty-five National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I female athletes (18-25 years old) were recruited; 21 completed the trial. In a randomized, double-blinded, placebo controlled, crossover design conducted over 4-8 weeks, participants consumed four treatments for three consecutive nights each: 40 g casein protein (CAS; 160 kcal), 40 g α-lactalbumin protein (ALA; 160 kcal), 40 g carbohydrate (CHO; 160 kcal), and 40g of a placebo (PLA; 5 kcal), with a minimum three-day washout between conditions. Supplements were consumed ~2 h after the final meal and ~30 min before bedtime as the last caloric intake of the day. Objective outcomes were obtained from the WHOOP 4.0 device (total sleep time (TST), sleep onset latency (SOL), sleep efficiency (SE), resting heart rate (RHR), and heart rate variability (HRV)). Subjective outcomes were assessed each morning via questionnaires (subjective sleep quality (SSQ), subjective sleep onset latency (SSOL), and subjective recovery (SREC)). Nocturnal interstitial glucose was assessed via blinded continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in a subset (n = 6). Sleep and recovery variables were analyzed using one-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) to evaluate treatment effects across the four supplementation conditions. For CGM data, a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA was used to evaluate main effects of treatment and time, as well as the treatment × time interaction. Tukey's post hoc testing was used with significance set at p < 0.05.
RESULTS: No significant treatment effects were observed for TST, SOL, SE, RHR, or HRV (p > 0.05). TST ranged from 7.47-7.62 h, SE from 91.5-92.0%, RHR from 53.5-54.1 bpm, and HRV from 98.2-103.9 ms across conditions. No significant treatment effects were detected for SSQ, SSOL, or SREC (p > 0.05); SSQ ranged from 69-75%, SSOL from 16-20 min, and SREC from 61-66%. In the CGM sub-analysis, a main effect of time was observed for nocturnal glucose (p = 0.008), but no differences among treatments (p = 0.187) or a time × treatment interaction (p = 0.550) were detected.
CONCLUSIONS: In NCAA Division I female athletes, three consecutive nights of pre-sleep ingestion of CAS, ALA, or CHO did not impair objective or subjective measures of sleep or recovery compared with PLA. These findings demonstrate that pre-sleep feeding, regardless of macronutrient type, can be incorporated without negatively affecting sleep quality or recovery metrics.

title: Short-term Rhodiola rosea supplementation improves premenstrual symptoms, reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes: a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Premenstrual symptoms may negatively influence psychological readiness, cognitive-motor performance, and perceived exertion in female athletes. Rhodiola rosea (RR) is an adaptogenic herb that has been investigated for its potential effects on fatigue, stress tolerance, mood, and exercise-related outcomes. However, its effects on premenstrual symptoms and performance-related responses in female athletes remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effects of short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase on premenstrual symptoms, peripheral serum serotonin and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) concentrations, reaction time, perceived exertion, and aerobic performance-related indices in female taekwondo athletes with premenstrual syndrome (PMS).
METHODS: In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 24 female taekwondo athletes with moderate-to-severe PMS symptoms were randomly assigned to receive either 500 mg/day of standardised RR extract (n = 12) or placebo (n = 12) for 10 days during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase. Premenstrual symptoms were assessed using the Premenstrual Symptoms Screening Tool (PSST). Visual reaction time, peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations, time to exhaustion (TTE), estimated VO₂max, and rating of perceived exertion (RPE) were evaluated before and after the intervention. Data were analysed using analysis of covariance with baseline values as covariates.
RESULTS: Compared with placebo, RR supplementation significantly reduced several PMS symptoms, including irritability, depression, anxiety, social withdrawal, decreased concentration, hypersomnia, food cravings, crying, skin problems, and abdominal pain (p < 0.05). The RR group demonstrated faster reaction time compared with placebo (adjusted mean difference: -60 ms; p < 0.001). Peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations were significantly higher in the RR group than in the placebo group (p < 0.001). In addition, RR supplementation reduced post-exercise RPE (adjusted mean difference: -1.40 Borg units; p = 0.006). However, no significant differences were observed between groups in TTE or estimated VO₂max (p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase may improve selected PMS symptoms, visual reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes with PMS. Larger trials with hormonal confirmation of menstrual cycle phase, longer intervention periods, direct physiological measurements, and sport-specific performance assessments are required to confirm these findings.

title: Photobiomodulation versus ischemic preconditioning for protection against exercise-induced muscle damage: protocol for a randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) occurs after unaccustomed eccentric exercise and may impair muscle recovery. Preconditioning with photobiomodulation (PBM) or ischemic preconditioning (IPC) may mitigate EIMD; however, no study has directly compared their effectiveness. This study aims to compare the effects of PBM and IPC applied prior to eccentric exercise on indirect markers of EIMD and associated perceptual responses. We hypothesized that MVIC trajectories would differ among the PBM, IPC, and sham groups, with PBM expected to provide greater preservation of MVIC than IPC. A prospective, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial with concealed allocation, blinded outcome assessors and statistician, and intention-to-treat analysis will be conducted. Healthy men (18-35 years) will be randomly allocated to PBM, IPC, or sham groups (n = 15 per group). After the intervention, participants will perform an eccentric exercise protocol for the elbow flexors consisting of 30 repetitions using a dumbbell load numerically matched to maximal voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC) values, with 45-second rest intervals. The primary outcome will be MVIC. Secondary outcomes include rate of force development, delayed-onset muscle soreness, pressure pain threshold, ultrasound echo intensity, range of motion, perceived exertion, and affective responses. Outcomes will be assessed at baseline, immediately after exercise (only MVIC), and at 24-, 48-, and 72-hours post-exercise. The primary analysis will assess the group × time interaction on MVIC using linear mixed-effects models, while secondary outcomes will be analyzed exploratorily. This study will provide, to our knowledge, the first direct comparison between PBM and IPC as preconditioning strategies to attenuate EIMD. The findings may help determine the most effective and clinically applicable intervention by considering both physiological and perceptual responses, thereby supporting decision-making in clinical and sports settings.Trial registrationBrazilian Registry of Clinical Trials (REBEC), RBR-6gr5kf; registered February 19, 2020; amended August 26, 2026.

title: Feasibility and Preliminary Effects of AI-Generated Personalized Sleep Feedback in High School Female Soccer Players: Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adequate sleep supports mood regulation and injury prevention in high school female athletes; however, insufficient sleep is common in this population. Wearable devices enable continuous assessment of objective sleep metrics, but personalized feedback based on daily sleep data remains underexplored.
OBJECTIVE: This study evaluated the technical and operational feasibility of a multicomponent AI-supported mobile health (mHealth) intervention that delivered personalized sleep feedback to high school female soccer players. Sleep efficiency was the primary preliminary efficacy outcome; other sleep-related measures were secondary or exploratory outcomes, and mood state and sports injury severity were exploratory outcomes.
METHODS: We conducted a pilot randomized controlled trial among 25 high school female soccer players from a single team. The study briefing and system setup began on August 18, 2025, and the trial was retrospectively registered with the University Hospital Medical Information Network (UMIN) Clinical Trials Registry on April 7, 2026 (UMIN000061189). Weeks 1 to 4 constituted the baseline period. After the week 5 baseline questionnaires, participants were stratified by median baseline total sleep time (TST) and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index score and randomly allocated 1:1 to the intervention (n=12) or control (n=13) group. During weeks 6 to 9, the intervention group received GPT-4o-generated personalized feedback via LINE on days with valid prior-night Fitbit data, whereas the control group received daily nonpersonalized sleep information. Technical and operational feasibility outcomes included message delivery success, valid Fitbit wear nights, questionnaire completion, technical problems, adverse events, and privacy breaches. Secondary outcomes included TST, wake after sleep onset (WASO), subjective sleep quality, sleep difficulty, and daytime sleepiness. Deep, light, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep durations, mood state, and sports injury severity were exploratory outcomes.
RESULTS: All 25 participants completed the trial. Message delivery success and questionnaire completion were 100% in both groups. Median valid Fitbit wear nights were 26 (IQR 24-28) in the intervention group and 22 (IQR 15-26) in the control group. No major technical problems, adverse events, or privacy breaches occurred. Change in sleep efficiency, the primary preliminary efficacy outcome, favored the intervention group (Hodges-Lehmann between-group difference 2%, 95% CI 0.50%-4%; P=.046; r=0.35). Nominal between-group differences were also observed for the Japanese version of the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI-J) total score and sleep difficulty score and, among exploratory outcomes, REM sleep duration and total mood disturbance. No between-group differences were observed in TST, WASO, deep or light sleep duration, daytime sleepiness, or sports injury severity.
CONCLUSIONS: The multicomponent AI-supported mHealth intervention demonstrated technical and operational feasibility in this single-team setting. Preliminary, hypothesis-generating between-group differences were observed in sleep efficiency and selected subjective sleep and mood outcomes. These findings should not be interpreted as evidence of established effectiveness and require confirmation in a sufficiently powered trial.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: UMIN Clinical Trials Registry UMIN000061189; https://tinyurl.com/tw3d7aku.

title: Characterizing accuracy, retention, and dose-response of an 18-session real-time gait biofeedback program following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Individuals following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) commonly demonstrate aberrant walking biomechanics, characterized by a lesser first peak vertical ground reaction force (vGRF) during early stance. Gait biofeedback may address this deficit; however, the accuracy, retention, and dose-response characteristics of repeated training remain unclear.
METHODS: Thirteen individuals (8 females and 5 males; age 22.4 ± 3.4 years; 32.6 ± 18.7 months post-ACLR) completed 18 gait biofeedback sessions over 6 weeks. Participants completed rehabilitation and exhibited involved limb first peak vGRF ≤1.12 body weight (BW) during baseline assessment of treadmill walking. Bilateral, step-by-step visual biofeedback targeted a first peak vGRF of 1.15 BW. Feedback was continuous during sessions 1-10 and was partially tapered thereafter. Outcomes included first peak vGRF target accuracy, defined as the percentage of steps within ±1% of the 1.15 BW target, first peak vGRF during retention, and the estimated training dose required to achieve target loading.
FINDINGS: First peak vGRF target accuracy increased in both limbs from ∼13% during session 1 and plateaued by session 12 (20-25%). Retention testing of the involved limb showed significantly higher first peak vGRF than baseline beginning at session 3, with these improvements maintained through session 18. The median effective dose to achieve target loading was 5 sessions (95% confidence interval: 3-14 sessions).
INTERPRETATION: Bilateral first peak vGRF target accuracy improved across training, while involved-limb improvements were retained before completing the 18-session protocol. These findings support the feasibility of shorter gait biofeedback regimens and provide clinically relevant dosing parameters to inform future clinical trials.

title: Screening-based low energy availability risk, disordered eating risk, and their co-occurrence among female volleyball players: a cross-sectional study.
abstract: Low energy availability (LEA) and disordered eating (DE) are important health concerns in female athletes, yet their occurrence and co-occurrence in team-sport contexts, particularly volleyball, remain underexplored. This cross-sectional online survey study examined the proportions of athletes classified as being at risk of LEA and DE overall and across competition levels, and assessed the co-occurrence between the two risk classifications in female volleyball players in Türkiye, using the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q) and Eating Attitudes Test-26 (EAT-26). It also examined correlations between EAT-26 total score and LEAF-Q total and domain scores. A total of 213 athletes, recruited via non-probability convenience sampling, completed the LEAF-Q and EAT-26 to assess LEA risk and DE risk, respectively. In this sample, 33.3% of athletes were classified as being at risk of LEA, with no difference across competition levels (p = 0.825). A total of 17.4% were classified as being at risk of DE, with variation across competition levels and the highest proportion among Turkish Women's Volleyball Second League athletes (p = 0.034). LEA risk and DE risk co-occurred in 10.3% of the sample, and DE risk was associated with higher odds of LEA risk (unadjusted OR = 3.80, 95% CI: 1.82-7.92). EAT-26 total score was positively correlated with LEAF-Q total and gastrointestinal function scores (p < 0.001) and injury history score (p = 0.004), but not menstrual function score (p = 0.133). These results suggest that LEA risk was commonly identified in this sample, DE risk was comparatively less common, and their co-occurrence was only partial, highlighting the value of screening for both risks rather than assuming one from the other.

title: Autologous Peripheral Blood-Derived Stem Cells Combined with Platelet-Rich Plasma is Associated With Clinical and Radiological Improvement in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Ruptures-Preliminary Clinical and MRI Findings in 47 Consecutive Patients.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) ruptures are common injuries in young and active individuals and can lead to long-term functional impairment and early onset osteoarthritis. While ACL reconstruction remains the standard of care, recent evidence suggests that spontaneous healing may be possible in selected cases. Regenerative and biologic treatment concepts have therefore gained increasing interest. This study investigates the clinical and radiological outcomes of a stem cell-based regenerative treatment for traumatic ACL ruptures and presents findings as preliminary observational evidence.
METHODS: In this single-center retrospective case series, 47 patients with isolated partial and complete traumatic anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) ruptures were treated using a biologic, non-surgical protocol. Diagnosis of an ACL rupture was confirmed by standardized clinical examination (Lachman test, anterior drawer test, and pivot shift test) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which was additionally used to assess rupture morphology and synovial sheath integrity. All patients underwent an ultrasound-guided injection of autologous biologic products derived from peripheral venous blood, consisting of 8 mL of an autologous blood-derived stem cell preparation (BSC), comprising approximately 2-3 mL of concentrated mononuclear cells suspended in 6 mL of autologous platelet-containing plasma, injected directly into the torn ACL. Patients were allowed immediate full weight-bearing without bracing and followed a standardized physiotherapy program. Clinical follow-up was conducted for 12 months, including assessment of pain (VAS), functional outcomes (IKDC, Lysholm), return-to-sport timelines, and MRI-based evaluation of ligament morphology.
RESULTS: The mean age of the cohort was 28.1 years (95% CI 26.0-30.2). Functional outcomes improved continuously throughout follow-up, with mean IKDC and Lysholm scores of 93.6 (95% CI 92.4-94.8) and 94.0 (95% CI 92.7-95.3), respectively, at 12 months. Pain levels decreased markedly, reaching a mean VAS score of 0.36 (95% CI 0.19-0.53). Patients returned to running after a mean of 2.19 weeks (95% CI 1.93-2.45), and most resumed their pre-injury activity level by one year. No infections or re-ruptures occurred and only one secondary ACL reconstruction was recorded. Patients with an intact synovial sheath demonstrated faster return to pivoting sports (26.8 vs. 33.2 weeks) compared with patients with a complete ACL rupture. MRI at 3 months showed evidence of improved ligament morphology in all but one patient.
CONCLUSIONS: This preliminary case series suggests that stem cell-based biologic stimulation may be associated with functional recovery and radiological improvement in selected patients with ACL ruptures. Prospective controlled trials are required to validate these findings.

title: Reliability of a functional electromechanical dynamometer for a bilateral standing press exercise at intensities of 30% and 60% of isometric peak force in trained women.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Determining the reliability of exercise instruments and protocols in the fields of health and sports performance is of great interest due to their close relationship with monitoring and decision-making in athletes. Studies in trained women are limited, and more evidence is needed on performance variables and the reliability of exercise protocols.
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the reliability of an exercise protocol for determining mean muscle strength, mean velocity, and mean power during the bilateral standing press (BSP) in trained women.
METHODS: Sixteen trained women (age = 20.0 ± 2.30 years; body mass = 67.63 ± 6.68 kg; height = 1.65 ± 0.06 m) participated in this repeated-measures study. Absolute reliability was assessed using the coefficient of variation (CV), and relative reliability was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for a bilateral standing press (BSP) exercise protocol performed at intensities of 30% and 60% of isometric peak force (IPF).
RESULTS: Mean muscle strength showed acceptable absolute reliability and extremely high relative reliability at both 30% IPF (CV = 6.51%; ICC = 0.94) and 60% IPF (CV = 5.03%; ICC = 0.97). Mean velocity showed extremely high relative reliability at 60% IPF (ICC = 0.92), but its absolute reliability was not acceptable at either 30% IPF (CV = 10.10%; ICC = 0.75) or 60% IPF (CV = 14.16%; ICC = 0.92). Mean power also exceeded the predefined CV threshold at 30% IPF (CV = 11.16%; ICC = 0.85) and at 60% IPF (CV = 14.35%; ICC = 0.89).
CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that the BSP protocol using functional electromechanical dynamometry is reliable for assessing mean muscle strength in trained women. However, mean velocity and mean power should be interpreted with caution, as their absolute reliability did not reach the predefined threshold of acceptable reliability.

title: Sleep-timing irregularity moderates the within-participant association between training load and next-morning heart rate variability in university sport participants: a 28-day study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Heart rate variability (HRV) describes beat-to-beat variation in cardiac intervals; the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD) is a time-domain index of short-term cardiac vagal modulation. We examined whether nightly deviation from habitual sleep midpoint moderated the association between prior-day internal training load and next-morning natural-log-transformed RMSSD (lnRMSSD), and whether analogous interactions were present for resting heart rate, wellness strain, and countermovement-jump (CMJ) height.
METHODS: University students engaged in regular sport training completed 28 days of habitual monitoring. Internal load was session duration multiplied by session rating of perceived exertion. Wrist actigraphy and sleep diaries estimated sleep midpoint, and 5-min morning RR recordings yielded lnRMSSD. Mixed models separated within- and between-participant components and tested within-participant load (per 100 arbitrary units [AU]) × absolute midpoint deviation (per 30 min).
RESULTS: The analysis included 1,232 mornings from 54 participants (57.4% female; age 21.0 ± 1.7 years). At each participant's mean midpoint deviation, greater-than-usual load was associated with lower next-morning lnRMSSD (β = -0.0089, 95% CI -0.0127 to -0.0051; p < 0.001). At mean load, greater-than-usual midpoint deviation was also associated with lower lnRMSSD (β = -0.0156, 95% CI -0.0268 to -0.0045; p = 0.006). The interaction was negative (β = -0.0101, 95% CI -0.0153 to -0.0048; p < 0.001). Thus, the inverse within-participant association between load and lnRMSSD strengthened as sleep-timing irregularity increased. No load-by-midpoint interaction was detected for resting heart rate, wellness strain, or CMJ height after false discovery rate adjustment. The primary interaction persisted after adjustment for prior-morning lnRMSSD (β = -0.0096, 95% CI -0.0147 to -0.0046; p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: The within-participant association between training load and next-morning cardiac vagal modulation was moderated by sleep-timing irregularity. These field-based associations do not establish a sleep mechanism, causal recovery effect, or decision threshold.

title: A Practical Pipeline for Patient-Specific Musculoskeletal Modeling: A Comprehensive MRI-Based Framework.
abstract: Patient-specific musculoskeletal (MS) modeling can provide estimates of internal joint loading that canot be measured directly. However, limitations in automated segmentation due to data-scarce environments, morphing difficulty caused by anatomical variability, and functional non-alignment are major bottlenecks that hinder the practical application of modeling and reduce productivity in musculoskeletal research. To comprehensively address these practical issues, this study proposes and validates an integrated, automated modeling framework.. First, we automatically segmented the lower extremity bones of the 4 knee osteoarthritis patients using a multi-atlas-based segmentation algorithm. By integrating the segmented bone with motion capture and force plate data, a modeling pipeline including multi-stage morphing and functional alignment processes was implemented. Using the constructed customized model, the medial and lateral knee contact forces (FMC and FLC) were estimated during a single-leg step-up exercise, and these were compared and evaluated against the results based on manual segmentation. The contact forces estimated through the automated segmentation framework demonstrated high consistency with the manual results. The mean absolute error ranged from 0.04 ± 0.03 to 0.06 ± 0.03 BW for FMC, and from 0.06 ± 0.04 to 0.09 ± 0.07 BW for FLC, and the intraclass correlation coefficient demonstrated a high correlation of over 0.99 across all patients. This study demonstrated that the proposed automated pipeline provides a practical approach to address misalignment caused by anatomical variability, while generating joint load estimates equivalent to the manual approach. By addressing key methodological challenges, this study will bring patient-specific models closer to future clinical application, where they could help assess individual loading across different activities and inform treatment and rehabilitation strategies.

title: A multimodal framework to assess differences in dynamic visual acuity between athletes with and without recent sport-related concussion.
abstract: Sport-related concussions (SRC) commonly affect vision and cognition, but there is limited understanding of how concurrent balance and exertion demands may affect visual-cognitive performance beyond symptom resolution.Purpose To determine if a dynamic visual acuity (DVA) task performed during standing and walking could differentiate performance between athletes with and without concussion history.Methods Interuniversity athletes (N = 30, age = 20.9 years ± 1.4) with SRC history who were asymptomatic (SRC = 14; females = 6) were compared to athletes without SRC (CONTROL = 16; female = 7). A DVA task was completed while seated, standing, and during low- and moderate-intensity treadmill walking. A Tumbling 'E' target was presented randomly in either random walk (R) or horizontal (H) motion (2.31 m/s), in one of four orientations; responses were selected using a handheld keypad. Performance was characterized as a change in DVA score from Seated (logMAR) and response time (RT, ms). A linear mixed-effects model was fitted for DVA change scores and a generalized mixed effects model for median RT.Results The SRC group exhibited worse DVA change scores during standing and walking compared to CONTROL (p < .05) during R-motion only. Whereas both groups responded faster during treadmill walking for both R- and H-motion (p < .001). Only two athletes (14%) in the SRC group experienced mild symptoms that did not affect performance during the protocol.Conclusion A multimodal DVA assessment, including standing and walking conditions, may be a feasible approach to detect differences in visual-cognitive performance for athletes following clinical recovery of concussion.

title: Recorded Adverse Events and Patient-Reported Outcomes After Intra-articular Extracellular-Vesicle Product Administration for Knee Osteoarthritis: A Retrospective Single-Practice Case Series.
abstract: Background Exosome-based products are being used for symptomatic knee osteoarthritis (OA), although human efficacy data remain limited and no extracellular vesicle product is approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration for intra-articular use. This study evaluated patient-reported outcomes, subsequent interventions, conversion to total knee arthroplasty (TKA), and recorded adverse events following intra-articular treatment. Objective The aim of the study was to compare pre-injection Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score for Joint Replacement (KOOS-JR) scores with scores obtained at six weeks and at the latest follow-up, and to document subsequent conversion to TKA. Study design This retrospective case series provides Level IV evidence. Methods Consecutive intra-articular knee treatments administered between December 2024 and August 2026 were retrospectively reviewed. Patients received either Patient Pure X (PPX™), an autologous platelet-derived extracellular-vesicle preparation, or DayZero™, an allogeneic perinatal tissue-derived extracellular-vesicle preparation manufactured by ZEO ScientifiX. For the primary patient-level analysis, one eligible index knee per patient was included to preserve independence of observations; laterality-ambiguous bilateral KOOS-JR observations were excluded from knee-specific patient-reported outcome analyses. Primary outcomes were paired changes in KOOS-JR from baseline to six weeks and latest follow-up. Secondary outcomes included subsequent nonsurgical interventions, subsequent TKA, and documented administration-related adverse events. Paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used. Results Fifty-one treated knees in 47 patients were included. Mean age was 75 years (range, 44-94 years); 28 patients were women, and 19 were men. In the primary patient-level analysis, 33 patients had complete, laterality-attributable paired baseline and six-week KOOS-JR data. Mean KOOS-JR increased from 60.0 to 78.5, a mean increase of 18.5 points (95% CI, 13.2-23.8; p<0.001); 30 of 33 patients (90.9%) had higher scores. At the latest follow-up, 36 patients had complete paired data; mean KOOS-JR increased from 60.6 to 77.4, a mean increase of 16.8 points (95% CI, 11.4-22.3; p<0.001), with 30 of 36 patients (83.3%) having higher scores. Three of 47 patients subsequently underwent TKA. No administration-related adverse events were documented in the available practice records; however, adverse-event ascertainment was retrospective. Conclusions In this retrospective single-practice case series, mean KOOS-JR was 18.5 points higher at six weeks than at baseline among 33 patients with complete, laterality-attributable paired data following intra-articular administration of extracellular-vesicle products. Later outcome assessments were limited by nonuniform follow-up and subsequent treatments. Three of 47 patients subsequently underwent TKA. No administration-related adverse events were documented in the available practice records; however, retrospective ascertainment and the limited sample size preclude conclusions regarding safety or tolerability. These descriptive findings do not establish efficacy, clinical importance, comparative effectiveness, structural disease modification, or long-term benefit. Prospective controlled studies using well-characterized products, standardized follow-up, prespecified management of subsequent interventions, and active adverse-event surveillance are warranted.

title: Timing Matters: Assessing Fatigue During and After Resistance Training.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Monitoring neuromuscular fatigue during resistance training informs load prescription and recovery management. Two common approaches, namely within-training assessment (immediately after each set) and post-training assessment (after session completion), differ in their methodological demands, yet their acute responses and within-session reliability remain insufficiently characterized.
HYPOTHESIS: Fatigue levels would be influenced by training protocol, value type (maximum vs average), and set number or timepoint, with corresponding differences in within-session reliability.
STUDY DESIGN: Randomized, counterbalanced crossover study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 2.
METHODS: A total of 13 well-trained male athletes completed 3 protocols in randomized order: 5 sets of fixed-repetition squats (Fixed), 5 sets of velocity-loss-threshold-controlled squats (VLT), and a control condition. Countermovement jump (CMJ) height was assessed at baseline, after each set, and at 8 post-training timepoints (5-60 minutes). Fatigue was quantified as the percentage of CMJ height relative to baseline, using both maximum and average values of 2 trials. Within-session reliability was evaluated via coefficient of variation (CV) and intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC).
RESULTS: For within-training assessment, significant main effects emerged for protocol (P = 0.006), value type (P = 0.031), and set number (P < 0.001), with lower values (greater fatigue) observed when using average values and in the final 2 sets. All protocols demonstrated acceptable within-session reliability (CV ≤ 5.29%, ICC ≥ 0.745). For post-training assessment, time point significantly affected fatigue (P < 0.001), with the lowest values at 30 to 40 minutes. ICC was low during 0 to 15 minutes post-training; acceptable reliability was achieved only with maximum values from 10 minutes onward (CV ≤ 7.29%, ICC ≥ 0.750).
CONCLUSION: Both within-training and post-training fatigue assessments are feasible for monitoring resistance training fatigue, but methodological choices substantially influence measured values and reliability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For within-training fatigue monitoring, average values provide greater sensitivity in detecting fatigue; for post-training assessment, maximum values should be used after ≥10 minutes of rest to ensure acceptable reliability.

title: Effects of adding sustained natural apophyseal glides on neuropathic pain-related symptoms and clinical outcomes in patients with lateral elbow tendinopathy: A randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cervical spine dysfunction and neural mechano-sensitivity may contribute to persistent symptoms in lateral elbow tendinopathy (LET), suggesting a potential role for cervical intervention such as sustained natural apophyseal glides (SNAGS) as an adjunct to rehabilitation.
PURPOSE: To investigate whether adding cervical SNAGS to a conventional rehabilitation program (CRP) improves neuropathic pain-related symptoms and signs, pain intensity, handgrip strength, pinch strength, and disability in individuals with LET.
METHODS: Arandomized controlled trial was conducted on52 participantswith unilateral LET, randomlyassigned toa study grouporcontrol group. The control group received aCRP, whereas the study group received the same program plus cervical SNAGS.Both groups were treated twice weekly for 4 weeks. Outcomes includedLeeds Assessment of Neuropathic Symptoms and Signs(LANSS), handgrip strength (HGS),lateral pinch strength, fingertip pinch strength, Numeric Pain Rating Scale (NPRS) at rest and during activity, and Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation (PRTEE). Outcomes were assessed before and after treatment.
RESULTS: Both groups demonstrated significant pre-to-post improvements across all outcomes (p < .001). Between-group analysis of change scores favored the study group for LANSS (p = .049, r_rb = 0.314), HGS (p < .001, r_rb = 1.000), lateral pinch strength (p < .001, r_rb = 1.000), and PRTEE (p = .001, r_rb = 0.521). No significant between-group differences were found for fingertip pinch strength (p = .343, r_rb = 0.152), NPRS at rest (p = .089, r_rb = 0.277), or NPRS during activity (p = .067, r_rb = 0.283). Baseline-adjusted analysis favored the study group for LANSS (p = .008), HGS (p < .001), lateral pinch strength (p < .001), fingertip pinch strength (p = .001), NPRS during activity (p = .034), and PRTEE (p = .001), whereas NPRS at rest did not differ significantly between groups (p = .105).
CONCLUSION: Adding cervical SNAGS to a CRP resulted in greater short-term improvement in several clinically relevant outcomes in individuals with LET.These findings support cervical SNAGS as a useful adjunct within a multimodal rehabilitation approach for LET.Clinical Trial Registry number: Prospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06271915).

title: Effect of tangeretin supplements on simulated precompetition weight loss in female combat sports athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Weight reduction before competition has long been a major challenge for combat-sports athletes. Unscientific weight-loss practices not only increase the risk of hormonal imbalance, electrolyte disturbance, and impaired immune function but also compromise athletic capacities such as aerobic and anaerobic performance and explosive power. This study investigated the potential benefits of tangeretin, a natural citrus extract, on athletic performance. These benefits include the regulation of hormone secretion, the optimization of carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, and the promotion of muscle synthesis and lipid utilization, which may help athletes reach their target weight.
OBJECTIVE: To examine the effects of tangeretin supplementation on body-composition and sports-performance indicators in female combat-sports athletes, and to evaluate its efficacy for simulated precompetition weight loss.
METHODS: Thirty female combat-sports athletes (4 wrestlers, 3 boxers, 9 sanda athletes, 3 judokas, and 11 taekwondo athletes) were recruited. A paired, randomized, double-blind design was used. All 30 participants were first paired according to sport and competitive level, then randomly allocated to either a tangeretin group or a placebo group (15 per group). The 30-day intervention comprised a double-blind nutritional supplement, a dietary questionnaire, blood sampling and analysis, body-composition assessment, isokinetic muscle-strength testing, and aerobic-capacity testing, to evaluate the effects of tangeretin (400 mg/day) on performance and health-related outcomes. These outcomes included body-composition indicators (e.g. body-fat percentage, fat mass, lean-body mass), fat-distribution indicators (e.g. limb and regional fat mass, gynoid fat mass), glucose and lipid-metabolism indicators (e.g. LDL-C, total cholesterol, free fatty acids), hormone indicators (e.g. cortisol, testosterone), muscle-strength indicators (e.g. peak torque of hip, knee, and ankle flexors and extensors), and maximal-oxygen-uptake-derived indicators (e.g. VO2max heart rate, time to exhaustion). Statistical significance was assessed using two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA).
RESULTS: (1) Body weight: 80.0% of athletes in the tangeretin group lost weight to varying degrees, and 33.3% (5 athletes) reached their competition weight class. (2) Body fat: body-fat percentage in the tangeretin group decreased from 23.92 ± 0.87% to 22.92 ± 0.89%; trunk, upper-limb, lower-limb, and android-region fat mass decreased by 6.77%, 8.77%, 4.43%, and 8.09%, respectively. (3) Glucose and lipid metabolism: HDL-C increased by 8.86% (P = 0.002), whereas triglycerides decreased by 25.00% (P = 0.048). (4) Sports performance: peak torque during hip, knee, and ankle flexion and extension increased significantly in the tangeretin group. VO2max also improved from 42.80 ± 1.13 to 43.46 ± 1.32 ml/kg/min.
CONCLUSION: Tangeretin supplementation effectively reduced body weight and fat mass (both overall and regionally) in female combat-sports athletes. Among the participants, 80.0% lost weight to varying degrees, and 33.3% reached their competition weight class, indicating a strong effect on precompetition weight loss. Moreover, tangeretin improved aerobic capacity and lower-limb joint muscle strength, thereby enhancing competitive performance.
