title: Effects of Integrative Neuromuscular Training on Unilateral and Bilateral Lower-Extremity Sports Performance in Adolescent Female Sprinters: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adolescent female athletes often exhibit more pronounced lower-limb asymmetry due to physiological differences, increasing injury risk. Despite documented efficacy in team sports for injury mitigation and performance enhancement, integrative neuromuscular training (INT) effects on unilateral and bilateral lower-limb capabilities in trained adolescent female sprinters remain undetermined.
HYPOTHESIS: We hypothesized that an 8-week INT program would significantly improve unilateral and bilateral lower-extremity performance measures in adolescent female sprinters compared with traditional sprint-specific training.
STUDY DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 1.
METHODS: Twenty-four national second-level adolescent female sprinters (aged 16-18 years) were randomly assigned to an 8-week INT group (n = 12) or a control group (CON, n = 12) that continued traditional sprint-specific training. Measurements obtained before and after the intervention included the hop test, star excursion balance test (SEBT), 3-repetition maximum (3RM) unilateral and bilateral back squat, 100-m run, standing long jump (SLJ), and limb symmetry index (LSI).
RESULTS: After the intervention, the INT group outperformed the CON group on the nondominant side in all hop tests (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.74-0.88), six directions of the SEBT (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.44-0.88), and the 3RM unilateral back squat (P < 0.01; ηp² = 0.65). On the dominant side, the INT group also outperformed the CON group in the single hop for distance (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.80) and three directions of the SEBT (P < 0.01; ηp² = 0.38-0.84). In addition, the INT group showed significantly greater improvements than the CON group in the LSI from unilateral tests (all P < 0.01; ηp² = 0.26-0.88), as well as in the 100-m run and SLJ (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.61-0.69).
CONCLUSION: The 8-week INT program was associated with improvements in dynamic balance, explosive power, and limb symmetry in adolescent female sprinters, with greater benefits observed on the nondominant side.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: INT is an effective training modality for improving lower-limb performance and mitigating asymmetry in adolescent female sprinters.

title: Refining Home-Based Squat Training: The Role of Hip Adduction in Improving Neuromuscular Control for Clinically Diagnosed Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome.
abstract: BACKGROUND Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) often stems from neuromuscular imbalances, particularly vastus medialis obliques (VMO) dysfunction impairing patellar tracking. Research is shifting toward integrated rehabilitation strategies, such as combining hip adduction with squats to enhance VMO recruitment. MATERIAL AND METHODS Thirty participants with PFPS were randomized to traditional squatting (SQU, n=15) or squatting with hip adduction (SQU-HA, n=15) for an 8-week home-based program with identical stretching. SQU-HA squeezed a Swiss ball during squats. Fifteen healthy individuals served as a reference group (RG). Outcome measures assessed before and after intervention included Q-angle, patellar tilt, clinical scales (visual analog scale [VAS], patellofemoral pain severity scale [PSS]), and electromyographic parameters (VMO, vastus lateralis [VL], adductor [ADD] amplitudes, onset times, VMO/VL ratio, and VMO-VL onset difference). RESULTS Both PFPS groups showed significant improvements in VAS and PSS after intervention, with greater VAS improvement in the SQU-HA group (P<0.01). Within-group analysis showed reduced patellar tilt in the SQU-HA group (P=0.003); between-group comparison did not reach statistical significance (P=0.217). Muscle activation onset sequences shifted from an abnormal pattern, in which VL activation preceded VMO and ADD activation, to a more typical pattern, in which VMO activation preceded VL and ADD activation. This shift was particularly evident in the SQU-HA group, whose activation pattern resembled that of the RG after intervention. Only VMO-VL onset difference, VMO/VL ratio, and Q-angle were correlated with clinical outcomes (P<0.05). CONCLUSIONS An 8-week SQU-HA program demonstrates promising short-term improvements in VMO-related neuromuscular measures and pain reduction for patients with PFPS. This accessible motor re-education strategy serves as a practical, home-based approach to patellofemoral rehabilitation.

title: Conservative management of carpal tunnel syndrome during pregnancy and lactation: A systematic review of mixed study designs.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pregnancy-related carpal tunnel syndrome (PRCTS) is the most common entrapment neuropathy during pregnancy, caused by gestational hormonal changes and fluid retention leading to increased intracarpal pressure and median nerve compression. Although symptoms often resolve postpartum, many patients experience significant functional impairment. Conservative treatment is preferred due to maternal-fetal safety concerns, but comparative evidence across modalities remains heterogeneous. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of conservative and minimally invasive interventions for PRCTS.
METHODS: The review protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261308958). A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library was conducted from database inception to 24 November 2025 (full search strategies in Supplementary Table S1). Studies evaluating conservative or minimally invasive treatments for CTS during pregnancy or lactation were included, irrespective of study design; case reports and case series without a comparator group were excluded a priori. Two independent reviewers performed study selection, data extraction, and methodological quality assessment using the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Quality Assessment Tools selected according to study design, and outcome-level certainty of evidence was additionally rated using the GRADE approach. Because of clinical and methodological heterogeneity, meta-analysis was not feasible; findings were synthesized qualitatively and supplemented with descriptive pooled summaries of reported outcomes by intervention.
RESULTS: Twelve studies met inclusion criteria. Night wrist splinting consistently improved symptoms in mild-to-moderate cases, particularly when combined with nerve and tendon gliding exercises. Ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injections provided effective short-term symptom relief in severe or refractory cases and appeared acceptable based on limited available evidence; however, no formal safety analysis was possible. Evidence supporting adjunct therapies, including kinesio taping, cupping, and laser therapy, was limited and inconsistent. Certainty of evidence, rated using GRADE, was low to very low for all principal outcomes, reflecting small sample sizes, methodological heterogeneity, and imprecision (Table 1b).
CONCLUSION: Night splinting remains the first-line treatment for PRCTS, with corticosteroid injection as a potential option for refractory cases when benefits outweigh risks. Further high-quality studies are needed to establish standardized treatment protocols and long-term maternal-fetal safety.

title: Reflections on 20 Years of Research on Tai Chi for Chronic Musculoskeletal Pain: An Updated Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Chronic musculoskeletal pain (CMP), including osteoarthritis (OA), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), fibromyalgia, and chronic low back pain (cLBP), contributes substantially to disability and reduced quality of life. Contemporary pain science supports biopsychosocial, multimodal management addressing nociceptive, neuropathic, and nociplastic mechanisms. Tai Chi is a multicomponent mind-body exercise integrating gentle movement, breathing, relaxation, balance, and attentional focus. This narrative review summarizes approximately 20 years of research on Tai Chi for CMP and considers its evolving evidence in contemporary rheumatology and pain management.
RECENT FINDINGS: Findings are strongest for knee and hip OA, with randomized trials and systematic reviews demonstrating improvements in pain, mobility, physical function, and stiffness compared with non-exercise controls. For cLBP, studies suggest potential improvements in pain and physical function, although heterogeneity and limitations in the certainty of evidence warrant cautious interpretation. In fibromyalgia, Tai Chi may improve pain and selected symptoms, but findings remain variable and the certainty of evidence is limited. In RA, research is sparse and inconsistent, with insufficient data to establish clinically meaningful effects on disease activity, pain, or physical function. Across conditions, Tai Chi has a generally favorable safety profile, although variations in interventions and outcome measures limit direct comparisons. Over two decades, research on Tai Chi for chronic musculoskeletal pain has expanded from relatively small efficacy trials to larger randomized studies, as well as mechanistic and pragmatic investigations. Findings are most supportive for knee and hip OA, whereas evidence for cLBP and fibromyalgia remains promising but heterogeneous, with limitations in the certainty of evidence. Evidence for RA remains insufficient to draw firm conclusions. Overall, Tai Chi appears to be a feasible and generally safe nonpharmacological intervention that may complement multimodal management of musculoskeletal pain. Further high-quality studies are needed to establish the magnitude and clinical relevance of its benefits, determine comparative effectiveness and optimal dose and delivery, and evaluate longer-term outcomes.

title: Implementing exercise therapy for hip and knee osteoarthritis in the clinic: a best practice narrative review.
abstract: Major guidelines recommend exercise for hip and knee osteoarthritis (OA), yet few provide guidance on how to prescribe it. This narrative review synthesizes high-quality and clinically relevant evidence on exercise therapy for hip or knee OA, prioritizing systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials. Findings were summarized across nine topics, with a focus on translating the evidence into specific guidance for clinicians. Clinicians should consider measuring pain, physical function, quality of life, and global assessment for most patients with hip or knee OA. When educating about OA, clinicians should focus on what patients can do and avoid impairment-based language. Exercise therapy is safe and provides small to moderate improvements in pain and function, although effects appear smaller for hip OA than for knee OA. No exercise type has proven superior, nor has a dose-response relationship been established. Patients with higher baseline pain and poorer function may benefit somewhat more, but effects differ little across other patient characteristics, including comorbidity burden and radiographic severity. Whether increasing adherence leads to greater improvements in pain and function remains unclear, but helping patients start and sustain exercise remains a priority, given its wide-ranging health benefits. In-person, telehealth, and self-directed delivery can all improve pain and function, and they appear to offer benefits of similar magnitude. Overall, exercise is safe, with the most common adverse event being temporary muscle or joint soreness. Clinicians do not need to search for an optimal program but can instead build one around the patient's priorities, preferences, and needs.

title: Patient and healthcare professional perceptions of weight reduction in the treatment of knee osteoarthritis: A systematic literature review.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Weight reduction confers significant clinical benefits in knee osteoarthritis (OA) management. This systematic review examined patients' and healthcare professionals' (HCPs) perceptions of weight reduction for surgical, pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions, with emphasis on barriers to implementation.
METHOD: The review was conducted across Embase, MEDLINE, Cochrane, and PsycInfo for eligible studies using the Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome, Timeframe, and Study type framework.
RESULTS: The search identified 2134 publications; of these, 203 had full-text screening, with 46 studies included: 23 qualitative studies, 15 cross-sectional studies, 6 randomized-controlled trials, one quasi-experimental and one observational cohort study. Four main themes of barriers to weight reduction were identified, including limited knowledge, lack of access to interventions, OA-specific barriers to exercise, and non-OA-specific barriers to dieting and exercise. The patient-reported barriers included intrapersonal barriers (i.e., difficulty achieving weight reduction, lack of motivation), physical barriers (i.e., age, challenges with general movement), and social barriers (i.e., lack of social support). The HCP-reported barriers included knowledge barriers, communication barriers, and systemic barriers (i.e., time constraints and resource limitations). Both patients and HCPs had varying expectations and satisfaction levels regarding the impact and delivery of weight reduction interventions.
CONCLUSIONS: Despite broad recognition of weight reduction's benefits in knee OA, substantial barriers hinder adherence and implementation. Targeted strategies addressing patient-HCP communication, alongside enhanced education and training for both groups, are critical to improving weight reduction outcomes in this population. There is currently a gap in evidence around barriers to gastric surgery and pharmacological treatment specific to patients with knee OA.

title: Objective Return-to-Sport (RTS) Decision Frameworks for Adolescent Shoulder and Elbow Injuries: Tests, Thresholds and Exercise Targets.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adolescent shoulder and elbow injuries are increasing due to sports specialization and year-round training, yet return-to-sport decisions typically rely on adult-derived heuristics that fail to address the unique physiology, growth plate vulnerability, and recovery needs of developing athletes aged 10-19 years.
OBJECTIVE: This review proposes a novel, objective three-pillar RTS framework integrating: (1) foundational tissue capacity, (2) dynamic movement quality and neuromuscular control, and (3) sport-specific load tolerance. We synthesize current evidence to establish provisional, consensus-based adolescent thresholds and provide a practical bedside toolkit for immediate clinical implementation.
METHODS: We conducted a narrative synthesis of contemporary original evidence, consensus recommendations, and validation studies relevant to adolescent shoulder and elbow rehabilitation. Evidence was critically appraised for youth-specific validation, with explicit distinction between evidence-based interventions and emerging aspirational technologies requiring prospective adolescent cohort validation.
RESULTS: We propose a hybrid benchmarking model combining limb symmetry indices (LSI ≥90%) with population-referenced percentiles (≥25th percentile for age/sex/sport) as provisional, consensus-based thresholds. A three-stage progression is outlined: Clinic-ready (pain-free ROM, isometric IR/ER LSI ≥90%), Training-ready (dynamic rotational LSI ≥90%, preserved scapular kinematics), and Game-ready (sport-specific tolerance with 5% velocity loss during simulated exposure). We provide a low-resource bedside toolkit including belt-stabilized hand-held dynamometry, Closed Kinetic Chain Upper Extremity Stability Test (CKCUEST), Push-Up Plus, Athletic Shoulder positions, seated medicine-ball throw, and simple interval tolerance simulations with specific protocols and thresholds. A stepwise algorithm advances from capacity → movement quality → load tolerance with targeted remediation at each gate.
CONCLUSION: Moving beyond time-based or adult-derived heuristics, this objective multidimensional framework aligns tissue recovery with sport-specific demands through quantifiable metrics. While provisional thresholds require further adolescent validation, the framework offers an evidence-guided pathway that mitigates reinjury risk, restores performance, and supports safe reintegration into sport. Implementation requires adolescent-specific normative databases, stakeholder communication, and cost-effective technological integration for equitable adoption.

title: Orthobiologics in Focus: Current Evidence, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions, A Scoping Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Regenerative modalities are increasingly becoming part of orthopedic practice with the use of orthobiologic interventions. These interventions make use of biological approaches to help in repairing the tissues, mitigating nociception, and improving locomotor performance.
OBJECTIVE: The current scoping review is a review of the modern literature as of 2020-2025 on orthobiologic therapies. It examines their clinical effectiveness, the strength of supporting evidence, and the development of new progress in musculoskeletal pathology regenerative management.
METHODS: A systematic search in PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and WoS was done on the articles with their indexes dated between January 2020 and February 2025. The inclusion criteria were human and animal studies that utilized platelet-rich plasma (PRP), (MSCs), bone marrow aspirate concentrate (BMAC), and adipose-derived products strategies using a scaffold only. Synthesis and data extraction were conducted as per PRISMA-ScR standards.
RESULTS: Among the 1716 records that had been filtered, 81 studies met inclusion criteria. Most of them were randomized or comparative trials (77% Level I-II evidence), which are evidence of the high methodological quality. PRP was the most commonly researched modality, whereas MSC-based interventions were the most common.
CONCLUSION: PRP, MSCs, and BMAC are orthobiologic modalities, which are evidence-based and effective alternatives to promote musculoskeletal healing and regeneration. These interventions supplemented by conventional surgical procedures and rehabilitative interventions yield pain relief, functional restoration, and long-term joint maintenance in a spectrum of orthopedic complications.

title: Cardiovascular Effects Associated with the Female Athlete Triad: Emerging Evidence Statement from the Female and Male Athlete Triad Coalition.
abstract: This is an emerging evidence statement from the Female and Male Athlete Triad Coalition. This paper complements the 2025 updates to the Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statements addressing the State of the Science and Clinical Guidelines for Screening, Diagnosis, Treatment and Return to Play. This paper examines emerging evidence of cardiovascular alterations in Triad-affected female athletes with functional hypothalamic amenorrhea and functional hypothalamic oligomenorrhea, including vascular, hemodynamic, autonomic and lipid perturbations. The clinical significance of these surrogate markers of cardiovascular function and their long-term cardiovascular implications remain to be determined. Notwithstanding, the current work extends existing Triad frameworks by recognizing cardiovascular perturbations potentially associated with energy deficiency and hypoestrogenism as an important consideration in female athlete health. We outline an evidence-informed research framework, including longitudinal, dose-response, and multimodal assessments, to characterize the onset, magnitude, physiological significance, and reversibility of cardiovascular alterations in athletes with functional hypothalamic amenorrhea and functional hypothalamic oligomenorrhea. By integrating evidence from sports physiology, endocrinology, and cardiovascular medicine, this state-of-the-science synthesis provides a roadmap for future research, screening, and intervention strategies. It also underscores the importance of evaluating cardiovascular health as a potential component of the broader physiological consequences of energy deficiency, alongside menstrual dysfunction, and impaired bone health.

title: [Disordered eating behaviors and eating disorders among athletes II.].
abstract: Over the past two and a half decades, a substantial shift has occurred in the understanding of disordered eating and eating disorders among athletes. Research has gradually moved beyond the concept of the female athlete triad towards the model of relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs), which recognizes low energy availability as a key factor affecting both athletes' health and performance. The aim of this study is to review the international literature published between 2000 and 2025 on disordered eating and eating disorders in athletes, with particular emphasis on prevalence, the contemporary interpretation of risk factors, the development of the REDs concept, and current recommendations for screening, treatment, and prevention. A thematic narrative literature review was conducted using the PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Scopus databases. Publications and professional consensus statements addressing disordered eating, eating disorders, relative energy deficiency, screening, prevention, and multidisciplinary care in athletes were included in the analysis. The reviewed literature indicates that disordered eating behaviors are considerably more prevalent than clinically diagnosed eating disorders; however, both conditions adversely affect athletes' health and performance. The evidence also confirms that low energy availability is not exclusively associated with eating disorders but may also result from an imbalance between energy intake and exercise expenditure. The introduction of the REDs model substantially expanded the earlier female athlete triad concept by highlighting the involvement of male athletes, the role of psychological factors, and the multisystem consequences of low energy availability. Current international recommendations emphasize early identification, sport-specific risk assessment, and multidisciplinary care as the cornerstones of effective prevention and treatment. Contemporary approaches to nutrition-related problems in athletes consider disordered eating, eating disorders, and relative energy deficiency as interrelated conditions. The development of standardized multidisciplinary models of care consistent with current international recommendations would be warranted in Hungary. Orv Hetil. 2026; 167(42): 1702-1709.

title: Early sub-maximal quadriceps motor unit firing characteristics and six-month knee extensor strength after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a prospective longitudinal study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To determine whether quadriceps motor unit firing rates measured pre-operatively and during the first three months after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction are associated with isometric knee extensor strength at six months, and to explore the relationship between motor unit action potential (MUAP) amplitude and firing rate.
METHODS: Twenty-seven participants (15 female) underwent surface electromyography of vastus medialis and vastus lateralis during sub-maximal isometric knee extension from pre-operation to three months post-reconstruction. Six-month knee extensor MVC force was modelled using Bayesian regression and interpreted using a region of practical equivalence (ROPE; ±15 N). A secondary hierarchical analysis examined MUAP amplitude and firing rate.
RESULTS: Motor unit firing rate was not consistently associated with six-month knee extensor strength across time points and limbs. In the ACL reconstructed limb at two weeks, a 1-SD greater mean firing rate was associated with 45.8 N greater six-month strength (95% credible interval [CrI] - 18.5 to 114.6 N). Six-month strength was greater in the contralateral limb (β = 198.4 N, 95% CrI 171.6 to 225.1 N), in males (β = 184.3 N, 95% CrI 32.0 to 325.1 N), and with greater body mass (β = 119.9 N per 1-SD, 95% CrI 33.4 to 207.2 N). Greater relative MUAP amplitude was associated with lower firing rate (-3.7 Hz per 1-SD, 95% CrI -3.8 to -3.6 Hz).
CONCLUSIONS: Sub-maximal quadriceps motor unit firing rate was not consistently associated with later knee extensor strength, although a stronger positive association was suggested in the reconstructed limb at two weeks. Firing rate was strongly related to relative MUAP amplitude, and its predictive value for later strength appears limited.

title: Dose-dependent effects of sodium bicarbonate supplementation combined with sprint interval training on performance adaptations in basketball players: a randomized placebo-controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sprint interval training (SIT) effectively improves physical performance in team-sport athletes, while sodium bicarbonate (Sb) supplementation may enhance training adaptations. However, the dose-dependent effects of Sb during SIT remain unclear in basketball players. Therefore, this study examined the effects of two Sb doses combined with SIT on physical performance adaptations in basketball players.
METHODS: Forty trained male basketball players (age: 21.6 ± 2.0 years, height: 185.4 ± 3.5 cm, body mass: 84.1 ± 4.4 kg) were recruited and randomly assigned to four groups: SIT + 0.3 g·kg-1 Sb (n = 10), SIT + 0.45 g·kg-1 Sb (n = 10), SIT + placebo (PL) (n = 10), and control (CON) (n = 10). The intervention lasted four weeks during the preparatory phase of the season. Participants in the training groups performed SIT three times per week in addition to their regular basketball training. The SIT protocol consisted of four sets of ten 5-second maximal sprints, with 20 seconds of active recovery between repetitions and 2 minutes of rest between sets. All 40 enrolled participants successfully completed the 4-week intervention, resulting in a 0% dropout rate. Performance assessments conducted before and after the intervention included countermovement vertical jump (CMVJ), standing long jump (SLJ), 20 m sprint, Illinois change-of-direction speed (CODS), Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 1 (Yo-Yo IR1), and Wingate anaerobic power (peak power output [PPO] and mean power output [MPO]).
RESULTS: All training groups showed significant improvements in physical performance variables over time (p < 0.05). Significant group by time interaction effects were observed for all performance variables (p ≤ 0.001), indicating that the SIT groups showed more gains compared with the CON group. Both Sb supplementation groups demonstrated greater improvements than the SIT + PL group in CMVJ, SLJ, sprint performance, CODS, Yo-Yo IR1 distance, PPO, and MPO (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the SIT + 0.45 g·kg-1 Sb group exhibited significantly greater performance enhancements than the SIT + 0.3 g·kg-1 Sb group across all measured variables.
CONCLUSION: Four weeks of SIT improved performance in trained basketball players, with Sb supplementation providing additional dose-dependent benefits (0.45 > 0.3 g⋅kg-1). While the higher dose yielded superior adaptations, its practical application should be balanced against potential gastrointestinal discomfort and individual tolerance to ensure long-term athlete compliance.

title: Calf Injuries: Anatomy, Pathology, and Treatment.
abstract: Calf injuries are common in athletes and typically result in missed time from sport and activities of daily living. The three individual triceps surae muscles can be injured, with differing described mechanisms. Gastrocnemius or plantaris strains tend to occur during sudden explosive movement of the ankle from a dorsiflexed to a plantarflexed position with the knee in extension. Soleus strains typically occur from repetitive dorsiflexion of the ankle with the knee flexed. Imaging modalities such as magnetic resonance imaging and ultrasonography can be helpful in determining the location and grade of injury, which can aid in treatment and return to play timelines. Classically, these injuries have been graded as grade I, II, or III, with grade I having <10% muscle fiber disruption, grade II having >10 to 50% muscle fiber disruption, and grade III having 50 to 100% muscle fiber disruption. The mainstay of treatment for most calf strains is nonsurgical, with surgical management being rare but reported in the literature for isolated grade III ruptures of the medial head of the gastrocnemius. Return to sport and activities requires a graduated physical therapy program focused on restoring tissue length without excessive strain. Recent limited evidence has shown promising results with quicker return to activities and decreased pain with platelet-rich plasma injections.

title: Functional recovery of athletes through rehabilitation training after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This article aims to introduce neuromuscular electrical stimulation into rehabilitation training after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and to assess its impact on the functional recovery of the knee joint.
METHODS: Twenty athletes undergoing anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction were allocated into a neuromuscular electrical stimulation group (neuromuscular electrical stimulation + rehabilitation training) and a conventional group (conventional rehabilitation training) for a 10-week training program. Indicators such as Lysholm scores and thigh circumference were assessed before and after training for comparison.
RESULTS: After training, the neuromuscular electrical stimulation group demonstrated a Lysholm score of 86.56 ± 11.67 points, a thigh circumference on the affected side of 47.15 ± 2.56 cm, and an active knee flexion angle of 105.12 ± 9.87°. Moreover, the score of the Y-balance test under left- and right-foot support was 93.67 ± 0.43 and 91.72 ± 0.48 points, respectively. It achieved a 10-meter walk speed of 1.01 ± 0.15 m/s. It achieved a performance of 264.39 ± 29.36 cm in three consecutive single-leg jumps on the healthy side and a performance of 178.16 ± 21.26 cm on the affected side. Its anterior cruciate ligament return-to-sport after injury scale score was 84.21 ± 5.32 points. These outcomes were significantly superior to those of the conventional group.
CONCLUSIONS: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation combined with rehabilitation training yields positive effects on functional recovery after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, surpassing the outcomes of conventional rehabilitation training. This approach holds promise for practical application.

title: Perineural Release with or Without Balloon Decompression for the Treatment of Lumbosacral Discogenic Syndromes in Professional Athletes.
abstract: Background: Lumbosacral discogenic syndrome (LSDS) is a common cause of low back pain (LBP) and lower limb pain (LLP) in athletes, often resulting in impaired sporting performance and delayed return to sport (RTS). Evidence regarding minimally invasive interventions, such as epidural perineural release (PNR), remains limited in athletic populations. Aim: This study aimed to compare outcomes following PNR with versus without balloon decompression neuroplasty in athletes with LSDS. Methods: We conducted a retrospective review of PNR performed between 2019 and 2024 for the treatment of LSDS among professional athletes. Demographic, clinical, and outcome data were collected from medical records and follow-up assessments. Pain intensity was assessed using the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS), while patient-reported outcomes were evaluated using the EuroQoL-5D (EQ-5D). Additional outcomes included pain-free walking, standing, and sitting durations, and self-reported health scores. Results: A total of 33 patients who had one intervention were included. Significant improvements were observed in all pain, functional, and quality-of-life outcomes following treatment (all p < 0.001). Maximum, minimum, and average pain intensity decreased from 7.5 ± 1.7 to 2.8 ± 2.2, 3.8 ± 2.3 to 0.3 ± 0.7, and 5.6 ± 1.7 to 1.5 ± 1.2, respectively. All EQ-5D domains and quality of sleep also improved significantly (all p < 0.001). Pain-free walking, standing, and sitting durations increased significantly, from 24.8 ± 23.2 to 49.7 ± 26.7 min, 18.4 ± 20.0 to 44.1 ± 23.1 min, and 25.5 ± 23.7 to 44.6 ± 24.9 min, respectively (all p < 0.001). Self-reported health scores improved from 51.9 ± 22.6 to 83.0 ± 14.3 (p < 0.001). Conclusions: Epidural perineural release, with or without balloon decompression neuroplasty, was associated by significant improvements in pain, functional capacity, and quality of life among athletes with LSDS refractory to conservative management. These findings suggest that PNR may be a promising minimally invasive treatment option; however, controlled prospective studies are required to establish its effectiveness and determine the additional benefit of balloon decompression.

title: Calf Injuries: An Anatomy-Based Approach to Diagnosis, Management and Return to Sport.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Calf muscle injuries are common in athletes but represent a heterogeneous group of lesions involving different muscles and myoconnective structures. This review provides a practical overview of gastrocnemius-soleus injuries, with particular emphasis on how anatomical characterization can contribute to diagnosis, management and return-to-sport decision-making. It also examines the limitations of current evidence and the extent to which increasingly detailed imaging findings translate into clinically meaningful information.
RECENT FINDINGS: Advances in ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging have improved the identification of specific injury patterns involving the gastrocnemius and soleus. Recent studies support moving beyond a muscle-based diagnosis towards more precise characterisation of the myoconnective structures involved. However, evidence linking individual anatomical patterns to prognosis and return-to-sport outcomes remains limited and largely observational. Current rehabilitation approaches favour progressive, criteria-based loading rather than fixed timelines, while return-to-sport decisions increasingly integrate clinical recovery, functional capacity, sport-specific demands and acceptable risk. No validated calf-specific rehabilitation or return-to-sport criteria are currently available. Anatomical characterization provides a useful framework for understanding the heterogeneity of calf muscle injuries but should inform rather than determine clinical management. Rehabilitation should remain function-led and progressively restore the mechanical capacities required for sport, while return to sport should be considered a multifactorial decision rather than the result of isolated imaging findings, tests or predefined timelines. Future prospective studies should determine which anatomical features provide clinically relevant prognostic information and develop validated calf-specific functional and return-to-sport outcomes.

title: The Mum-Alete: An Observational Survey-Based Study of Australian Athletes Returning to High-Performance Sport After Pregnancy.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: As more female athletes extend their careers and resume high-performance sport following childbirth, there is an increasing need to understand factors influencing this transition. The return-to-high-performance sport process for postpartum athletes remains complex, with limited evidence available to guide sporting organisations and practitioners. This study aimed to identify the experiences, facilitators, challenges, and barriers for athletes returning to high-performance sport postpartum.
DESIGN: An exploratory cross-sectional survey study.
METHODS: Participants included postpartum elite and sub-elite Australian athletes who maintained training 6 months prior to conception and gave birth between July 2016 and February 2022. The online Mum-Alete survey included various types of closed-ended questions as well as open-ended questions to gather deeper insights related to demographic/pregnancy information, training and performance, physical health (e.g., sport-related injuries), and social factors impacting return to high-performance sport. Descriptive statistics were used to summarise data, while a hybrid thematic analysis was used for qualitative analyses.
RESULTS: Descriptive analyses for the 64 athletes who participated showed most resumed exercise within 6-week postpartum, with pelvic floor exercises initiated earliest. Endurance and strength training followed, though 59% of respondents reported performance declines and 43% reported sport-related injuries. Key challenges in returning to high-performance sport included time management, sleep, breastfeeding, and pelvic floor dysfunction. Among facilitators in returning to high-performance sport, support from family, coaches, and medical staff was generally rated positively, with many athletes reporting a lack of (or non-awareness of) organisational policies and support provisions (e.g., well-being officer, maternity leave, status protections, including stipends, caregiver allowance to attend training) as well as facility-related challenges (e.g., dedicated spaces for childcare and breastfeeding). Eight qualitative themes were identified, including time/time management, training 'new' bodies, safe return to high-performance sport, breastfeeding while participating, critical support, navigating motherhood and sport, discrimination, and education/expertise.
CONCLUSIONS: This study showed that while athletes returned to high-performance training relatively early following childbirth, they regularly perceived reductions in performance and reported sport-related injuries. Various factors were also shown to facilitate and challenge the return-to-high-performance sport process. These outcomes highlight the need for athlete-informed, multidisciplinary, and flexible support strategies, and underscore critical gaps in organisational practice.

title: Artificial intelligence across the continuum of care for the aging musculoskeletal patient: From longitudinal phenotyping to personalized surgery and recovery monitoring.
abstract: Musculoskeletal care is being reshaped by population aging, multimorbidity, frailty, osteoporosis, sarcopenia, polypharmacy and increasing vulnerability to postoperative loss of independence. Artificial intelligence (AI) has entered orthopaedic research, but its clinical translation remains constrained. Many models address isolated diagnostic, imaging or short-term prediction tasks rather than the longitudinal care trajectories that determine outcomes in older musculoskeletal patients. The central limitation is therefore not simply whether older adults are represented in datasets, but whether AI systems are valid across the continuum of geriatric orthopaedic care. This review argues for a transition from task-specific orthopaedic AI toward continuum-of-care AI for the aging musculoskeletal patient. Upstream, radiomics, longitudinal osteoarthritis phenotyping, opportunistic computed tomography (CT)-based skeletal assessment and AI-augmented dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) modelling may improve prediction of disease progression, fracture risk, treatment failure and surgical timing. At the point of intervention, AI-assisted arthroplasty planning may help move total knee arthroplasty from generic alignment targets toward phenotype-specific reconstruction strategies that account for constitutional alignment, bone morphology, ligament envelope, neuromuscular control, frailty and functional reserve. Perioperatively, automated frailty and sarcopenia phenotyping, wearable gait analysis and multimodal temporal models integrating imaging, electronic health records, laboratory data, medications, patient-reported outcomes and wearable signals may support dynamic risk prediction. After discharge, continuous monitoring of mobility, sleep, pain trajectories, wound-related symptoms and rehabilitation adherence may help close the high-risk surveillance gap during the 90-day postoperative episode. However, clinical adoption requires more than high discrimination. Explainable AI should be understood as one component of a broader trust framework that also includes calibration, uncertainty quantification, decision-curve analysis, external and prospective validation, workflow integration, post-deployment monitoring and accountability. The future of orthopaedic AI is not simply better diagnosis or more precise surgery, but longitudinal, multimodal support across the full care continuum: predicting progression, selecting treatment, personalizing surgery, optimizing perioperative care, monitoring recovery and preserving mobility and independence. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV.

title: Multimodal Programming of Extracellular Vesicles via Nano-Primed SECCS-Based 3D Microenvironments for Coordinated Ferroptosis Suppression and Myogenic Regeneration in Diabetes.
abstract: Chronic diabetic glucolipotoxicity is associated with progressive skeletal muscle atrophy, bone loss, cellular senescence, and ferroptotic injury. Because ferroptosis inhibition alone may not restore compromised myogenic capacity, we developed a combined stem cell-conditioning strategy integrating fullerol priming with the stem cell screen-enrich-combine(-biomaterials) circulating system (SECCS). This integrated three-dimensional culture platform uses porous β-TCP granules and intermittent medium circulation to generate BMSCs-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs). Among 2D-EVs, F-2D-EVs, SECCS-EVs, and F-SECCS-EVs, F-SECCS-EVs exhibited the strongest anti-ferroptotic and pro-regenerative effects. In glucolipotoxicity-challenged myoblasts, F-SECCS-EVs attenuated ferroptotic injury and enhanced proliferation and myogenic differentiation. Transcriptomic and functional experiments identified FOXO3 as an important mediator linking antioxidant defense with myogenic programs. In diabetic mice, F-SECCS-EVs improved motor function, muscle strength, myofiber cross-sectional area, and myogenic marker expression while modulating macrophage polarization. Free fullerol, 2D-EVs, and F-2D-EVs produced limited recovery, whereas SECCS-EVs were less effective than F-SECCS-EVs. These muscle benefits were accompanied by favorable changes in tibial bone structure. Collectively, these findings support fullerol-primed SECCS culture as a strategy for coordinating ferroptosis control with myogenic recovery in diabetes-associated musculoskeletal degeneration.

title: A Narrative Review on Intra-Articular Injection Therapies for Knee Osteoarthritis: Current Evidence and Future Perspectives.
abstract: This narrative review summarises current evidence on intra-articular injection therapies for knee osteoarthritis. Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a major global cause of disability, particularly among older adults, prompting growing interest in non-operative strategies that alleviate symptoms, preserve joint function, and delay surgical intervention. Established options including corticosteroids and hyaluronic acid, remain widely utilized for short and intermediate-term symptom relief. Regenerative approaches such as platelet-rich plasma (PRP) and mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have gained prominence due to their potential anti-inflammatory and reparative effects. Novel biologic agents, including exosomes, atelocollagen, and isolated growth factors, show promise in supporting tissue repair and modulating joint homeostasis. Given the wide variability in mechanisms, efficacy, and safety profiles, selection of treatment regimen should be individualized based on disease severity, patient goals, and regulatory considerations. Overall, intra-articular injection therapies represent a diverse and rapidly evolving component of knee OA management. Continued high-quality randomized trials and standardized treatment protocols are essential to support evidence-based clinical decision-making and optimize patient outcomes.

title: Ergogenic effects of beetroot juice supplementation on neuromuscular function and simulated combat demands in elite female taekwondo athletes.
abstract: Beetroot juice supplementation has been widely examined across various sport disciplines due to its potential ergogenic effects. However, evidence regarding its impact on combat sports particularly in female athletes remains limited. The aim of this study was to evaluate the acute effects of beetroot juice supplementation on simulated taekwondo combat performance and neuromuscular function in elite female taekwondo athletes. Seven elite female Olympic taekwondo athletes (age: 20.3 ± 3.7 years), participated in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study consisting of two experimental trials). Each trial involved the consumption of either 140 mL of beetroot juice (which contains 12.8 mmol NO₃⁻) or 140 mL of a placebo (with 0.08 mmol NO₃⁻) followed by a simulated taekwondo combat session and assessments of neuro-muscular function (i.e., vertical jump and visual cognitive performance). In addition, metabolic (i.e., blood lactate), and perceptual responses (i.e., rate of perceived exertion) were measured before, after, and 3 minutes post-combat. No significant differences during the simulated taekwondo combat (e.g., attack time; p = 0.531-0.989; ηp² = 0.01-0.05), neuromuscular function battery (p = 0.302-0.700; ηp² = 0.02-0.04), blood lactate concentrations (p = 0.705; ηp² = 0.13), or rate of perceived exertion values (RPE) (p = 0.717; ηp² = 0.12) were obtained between beetroot juice and placebo conditions. Acute ingestion of beetroot juice (140 mL) did not enhance simulated combat performance or neuromuscular function in female Olympic taekwondo athletes.

title: Physical examination of the cervical spine should be conducted in female athletes with a history of concussion.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Female athletes may be at increased risk of injury following sports-related concussion (SRC), even after symptom resolution. Residual cervical spine impairments have been proposed as a potential contributor; however, these have not been well characterised in female athletes. This study aimed to examine whether a history of SRC was associated with clinical assessments of the cervical spine in female athletes.
METHODS: In this cross-sectional observational study, 156 elite and pre-elite female athletes from water polo, soccer, diving, rugby-7s and cycling/BMX were recruited. History of SRC within the previous 12 months was self-reported. Assessments included questionnaires and physical examination of the cervical spine, comprising range of motion, manual examination, joint position error (JPE) and maximal isometric neck strength. Between-group differences were examined using univariable statistical analyses.
RESULTS: Athletes with a history of SRC demonstrated a higher prevalence of reduced cervical range of motion, positive findings on manual examination, increased JPE and a history of headaches or migraines compared with athletes without concussion history. No deficits in maximal isometric neck strength were observed in athletes with a history of SRC.
CONCLUSION: Cervical spine impairments were more commonly observed in female athletes with a history of SRC within the previous 12 months, including in athletes who did not report current neck pain. These findings suggest consideration of targeted cervical spine assessment beyond symptom-based screening in athletes with a concussion history. Whether identification and management of cervical spine impairments influence subsequent injury risk requires investigation in prospective and interventional studies.

title: Endocrine dynamics of special operations forces across mission cycles: implications for human stress physiology.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study investigates the endocrine responses and muscle damage markers in elite male Special Operations Force operators across operational phases to understand hormonal adaptations to extreme operational stress and recovery.
METHODS: Fifty-six operators (28-42 years) participated in a longitudinal study conducted at a Special Operations Forces unit. Blood samples were collected at three visits: Visit 1 (baseline recovery), Visit 2 (intensive pre-deployment training), and Visit 3 (post-deployment recovery). Serum concentrations of testosterone (T), cortisol (CORT), dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S), growth hormone (GH), insulin-like growth factor-I (IGF-I), progesterone (P4), creatine kinase (CK), and myoglobin (Mb) were analyzed.
RESULTS: Post-deployment (Visit 3), T levels increased (+ 20%, p < 0.05), and CORT decreased (- 23%, p < 0.05), resulting in a significantly higher testosterone-to-cortisol ratio compared with Visit 1 and Visit 2 (p ≤ 0.05). DHEA-S correlated with CORT (r = 0.37, p < 0.05), suggesting a compensatory adrenal response under stress. GH concentrations were markedly reduced post-deployment (- 84%, p ≤ 0.05), while IGF-I remained stable, indicating differential regulation within the GH-IGF-I axis during recovery. P4 concentrations remained elevated across all phases, reflecting a consistent endocrine feature across operational phases rather than a defined mechanistic adaptation. No significant changes were observed in CK or Mb, underscoring effective physical stress management at the time of post-deployment sampling.
CONCLUSION: These findings emphasize the importance of tailored training and recovery strategies for sustaining endocrine balance, resilience, and operational readiness in elite military personnel.

title: Integrated physical, cognitive and psychological rehabilitation following multiple ACL reconstructions in a professional handball player: a case report.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries with repeated surgical interventions and postoperative complications pose a major challenge in sports rehabilitation. Beyond neuromuscular deficits, psychological and cognitive readiness often remain impaired, increasing reinjury risk and threatening athletic careers. This case highlights an integrated rehabilitation strategy addressing physical, psychological, and cognitive domains in a professional athlete with a complex surgical history.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 31-year-old white Serbian male professional handball player with a history of two ACL reconstructions, meniscal repairs, a postoperative knee infection, and multiple arthroscopic interventions presented with persistent knee instability, pain, and psychological distress. Following repeated failed return-to-play attempts, he underwent a ten-week intervention combining therapeutic exercises, sports psychology sessions, and neurocognitive dual-task training. Pre- and post-intervention assessments included gait analysis, postural control, strength testing, ACL-specific functional tests, and psychological evaluations. Post-intervention assessments showed improvements in gait mechanics, postural stability, neuromuscular strength, and reduced functional asymmetries, alongside lower cognitive anxiety and greater motivation.
CONCLUSIONS: This case suggests that an interdisciplinary, multimodal rehabilitation approach, integrating physical, psychological, and cognitive strategies, may help address both physical deficits and psychological barriers in athletes with multiple ACL surgeries and complex postoperative courses. Such integration may support function, confidence, and readiness in high-performance athletes facing career-threatening injuries.

title: All-Suture Fixation for Acute Turf Toe Injuries.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Turf toe is a hallux metatarsophalangeal joint (MTPJ) injury caused by hyperextension of the great toe with axial loading1,2. High-grade injuries may threaten return to sport and require surgery3,4. Here, we describe a capsular reconstruction of the great toe MTPJ with all-knotless suture anchors and suture tape augmentation for turf toe injuries, in isolation or in combination with a traumatic bunion, designed to reduce suture burden, minimize soft-tissue irritation, and facilitate recovery.
DESCRIPTION: The procedure begins with the patient supine. A direct medial approach to the hallux MTPJ is performed. Both the medial base of the proximal phalanx and the medial eminence of the metatarsal head are drilled at isometric points, and augmentation with suture tape is then performed. Isometric drill holes are placed in the medial proximal phalanx base and metatarsal head for suture tape augmentation. A knotless suture anchor is placed approximately 3 mm proximal to the articular margin of the metatarsal head, repairing the medial capsule in a horizontal mattress fashion. An additional knotless anchor is placed at the plantar plate insertion, and the suture is passed through the tibial sesamoid sling and tensioned with the toe in 20° of plantar flexion. Suture tape is secured into the proximal phalanx with an interference screw, then passed through the deep capsule into the metatarsal head, followed by the placement of an additional interference screw into the metatarsal head. The anchor is inserted into the plantar-medial proximal phalanx at the flexor hallucis brevis insertion. The toe is flexed during tensioning, then adjusted per clinical examination and the sesamoid location beneath the metatarsal head. Knotless fixation permits incremental tensioning with intraoperative assessment of motion. Final tensioning is performed with the toe in neutral to correct deformity without overconstraint, preserving range of motion.
ALTERNATIVES: Nonoperative alternatives include rest, ice, compression and elevation; anti-inflammatory drugs; activity modification; and brief immobilization5,6. Operative alternatives include primary capsuloligamentous complex repair with nonabsorbable sutures, plantar plate advancement with bone tunnels or suture anchors if primary repair is not feasible, and concomitant procedures such as sesamoidectomy and bunionectomy based on the injury pattern2,7,8.
RATIONALE: This technique is intended for high-grade turf toe injuries with capsuloligamentous disruption, sesamoid complex insufficiency, and MTPJ instability. Nonoperative treatment may be appropriate in cases of low-grade injury; however, persistent pain, instability, or loss of push-off strength following nonoperative treatment would indicate a higher-grade injury. Compared with isolated repair or plantar plate advancement alone, this technique restores both static and dynamic stabilizers of the hallux MTPJ while addressing associated angular deformity. Suture tape augmentation resists recurrent hyperextension and valgus forces while allowing controlled physiologic motion. Knotless, low-profile suture anchors minimize bulk and hardware prominence in a region with limited soft-tissue coverage and bone stock. This construct offers a robust reconstruction option for athletes requiring predictable restoration of stability and reliable return to sport.
EXPECTED OUTCOMES: Operative treatment of high-grade turf toe injuries has been shown to result in reliable pain relief, restored stability, and high rates of return to sport8. Previous studies have suggested improved function and earlier return to play compared with prolonged nonoperative treatment in appropriate patients6,7. Knotless suture anchors reduce implant prominence and eliminate knot-related irritation, while the small insertional diameter of the suture anchors preserves bone stock in the metatarsal head and proximal phalanx. This construct provides immediate stability while allowing controlled motion, facilitating rehabilitation, and reducing postoperative stiffness. Athletes typically return to unrestricted activity within 6 to 9 months, aided by the suture tape augmentation allowing earlier movement through the range of motion. This augmentation reduces the need for long-term spica splinting and bracing and reduces the risk of recurrence.
IMPORTANT TIPS: The small anchor diameter and use of suture tape allow easy access without hardware burden.○ Suture choice depends on surgeon preference regarding construct stiffness and on the tissue quality and risk of irritation. We believe that suture tape lays flatter and, if required, knots are smaller.Avoid suture twisting or kinking, which can prematurely lock anchors, compromising fixation.○ After the anchor is placed, we keep the suture tape secured out of the field as we prepare the capsule with absorbable suture. As we load the second anchor, we maintain tension on the tape to prevent twisting.Overtightening the MTPJ capsule may lead to altered biomechanics.
ACRONYMS AND ABBREVIATIONS: RICE = rest, ice, compression, elevationMRI = magnetic resonance imagingBID = twice daily.

title: Spaceflight human optimization and performance: positioning astronauts in an operational framework to promote health, fitness, and mission readiness.
abstract: Optimizing astronaut mission readiness is a multidisciplinary endeavor that should integrate concepts from aerospace medicine, human performance, sports science, nutrition, and engineering. Situating astronauts within a theoretical framework similar to that of operational athletes, while addressing top human systems capability needs outlined for future missions, may be optimal for promoting sustained health and performance before, during, and after missions to low-Earth orbit, the lunar surface, and Mars. Mission readiness can be optimized by enhancing physiological and behavioral/psychological performance through data-driven and individualized exercise countermeasures, health and performance monitoring, precision nutrition, and rehabilitation strategies. Appropriate and stable space food systems that facilitate adequate provision of nutrients and fluids to prime astronauts for mission-critical tasks and operational demands are needed, though research is needed into potential nutritional considerations that might be useful for future missions. Behavioral readiness programs should emphasize stress inoculation, adaptive decision-making, communication, Earth-independent operation functionality, conflict resolution, leadership, and team-based problem-solving before flight to promote healthy team dynamics in-flight, along with proper society reintegration and uptake of family and occupational roles post-flight. Exercise remains an essential countermeasure during spaceflight, with an emphasis on maximizing fitness before launch to mitigate in-flight declines and on maintaining fitness levels and functionality during flight through high-intensity multimodal exercise. Following return to Earth, rehabilitative programs serve to restore cardiovascular, sensorimotor, and skeletal function, followed by enhancing skill-based performance components through a phase-based training program. Continuous monitoring systems that provide insight into health, performance, sleep, cognitive, nutritional, and recovery status should enable data-driven decision-making on physical readiness across all mission phases. By integrating insight from multiple disciplines, this unifying approach delivers a theoretical framework for sustaining astronaut health and performance during extended-duration missions.

title: Persistent and recurrent musculoskeletal pain in young athletes: an overlooked biopsychosocial determinant of return to sport trajectories - a focused narrative review.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Persistent and recurrent musculoskeletal pain is common in young athletes, yet its role in recovery and return to sport (RTS) decision-making remains insufficiently acknowledged. In youth sport, pain is often normalized or viewed primarily through an injury-centered lens, despite its potential to shape function, participation patterns, and athletic trajectories over time.
AREAS COVERED: This focused narrative review aimed to (1) synthesize current evidence on persistent and recurrent musculoskeletal pain in young athletes and (2) propose a developmentally informed biopsychosocial framework for understanding its implications for RTS. Electronic searches were conducted in PubMed, PsycINFO, and SPORTDiscus for studies published from 1 January 2006, through 28 February 2026, supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking and targeted hand-searching of reference lists. It integrates evidence on definitions, prevalence, clinical presentation, psychosocial and contextual factors, functional interference, and RTS decision-making, conceptualizing ongoing pain as an overlooked determinant of RTS trajectories.
EXPERT OPINION/COMMENTARY: In young athletes, pain should not be treated as a peripheral symptom or addressed only when recovery is delayed. More informed RTS decisions require attention not only to physical recovery markers, but also to how pain is experienced, interpreted, and managed throughout recovery. A developmentally informed biopsychosocial perspective may support earlier recognition, safer return decisions, more stable participation, and better long-term health outcomes.

title: Ultrasound-guided injection treatments for tendinopathy: an update.
abstract: The choice of treatment for chronic tendinopathy and related peritendinous conditions has become challenging as multiple options are available. When conservative treatments fail, injections of platelet-rich plasma (PRP), corticosteroids, and hyaluronic acid have become important in the management of these conditions. Other interventions, such as dry-needling, percutaneous tenotomy, percutaneous release, and hydrodissection, may also be used. Ultrasound guidance allows real-time visualization of the needle relative to its target and adjacent neurovascular structures. This is particularly advantageous for deep or small-caliber tendons, for procedures requiring precise intratendinous or peritendinous needle placement (e.g., PRP injection, hydrodissection), and for percutaneous release, where a blind approach carries a materially higher risk of neurovascular or tendon injury. This review summarizes the mechanism of action, technique, evidence, and indications for the injection treatments currently used for tendinopathy, and outlines the general principles of ultrasound-guided injection technique.

title: More than fuel: Why athletes need better language around food.
abstract: "Food is fuel" is a widely used phrase in sport settings intended to emphasize the importance of nutrition for performance. While nutrition is essential for health and success, this framing may unintentionally reinforce a narrow, performance-oriented understanding of eating that has implications for athletes' relationships with food and their bodies. Athletes are at heightened risk for eating concerns, low energy availability, and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs), and aspects of sport culture may contribute to rigid, rule-based approaches to eating. This commentary argues that "food is fuel" language reflects and reinforced broader sports norms centered around optimization, control, and performance. Potential consequences include reduced attunement to internal cues and the moralization of food choices, particularly in sport environments where appearance and performance are closely intertwined. Language is proposed as a modifiable factor for prevention and more flexible, athlete-centered approaches to discussing food and eating are identified. Rather than dismissing the importance of nutrition in athletics, this commentary advocates for broader conceptualizations of eating that acknowledge its physical, psychological, social, and cultural functions and support athletes in developing sustainable relationships with food throughout and beyond their athletic careers.

title: Prebiotics in sport and exercise: current evidence, practical applications, and methodological considerations.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prebiotics are selectively utilized by the host microbiota and can confer health and/or performance benefits, in part through increasing the abundance of beneficial gut microorganisms and their metabolites. While several studies have shown promising initial findings, high-quality scientific evidence examining the effects of prebiotics on athlete performance, health and wellbeing remains limited.
METHODS: This narrative review summarizes the current available evidence on prebiotic intake in athletic populations, including effects on gastrointestinal structure and function, immune responses, recovery, sleep, wellness, mood and exercise performance. In areas where there is limited evidence in athletic cohorts, but a physiological rationale for a benefit, findings from sedentary and/or clinical populations are evaluated, and the potential relevance of these findings to athletes are discussed. Finally, considerations for practitioners around the use of prebiotics with athletes are provided, and recommendations for designing future prebiotic-based research are explored.
RESULTS: Despite the limited existing literature around prebiotic use in athletes, there are several studies that indicate their potential to improve gut barrier integrity and reduce the incidence/severity of gastrointestinal symptoms. Data also indicates that prebiotics can increase salivary Immunoglobulin A secretion rate and reduce the duration and/or severity of upper respiratory symptoms in trained individuals. Other areas with emerging evidence that warrant further investigation in athletic populations include prebiotics' ability to support exercise adaptation and recovery, promote sleep improvements and enhance mood and cognitive function. The interpretation of current studies is limited by the lack of gut microbiome and metabolome measures and the absence of robust performance measures following a period of prebiotic supplementation. Well-controlled, adequately powered studies incorporating these outcomes are needed to determine the contexts in which prebiotic intake can meaningfully improve health and performance metrics, and to elucidate the underlying physiological mechanisms of any beneficial effects.
CONCLUSION: Prebiotic intake represents a promising intervention to attenuate exercise-induced disturbances to the intestinal epithelium, reduce exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms, and lower the duration/severity of upper respiratory symptoms in athletes. Future studies should prioritize high-quality performance assessments, alongside comprehensive microbiome and metabolome profiling, to elucidate mechanistic effects. Areas with limited current evidence such as recovery, sleep, mood, cognitive function, bone health and nutrient absorption in athlete cohorts should also be further explored.

title: Core Muscle Injury: A Combined Orthopaedic and General Surgery Algorithmic Approach for Diagnosis, Imaging, and Treatment.
abstract: » Core muscle injury (CMI) is a common cause of groin pain in athletes and reflects pathology of the inguinal canal, rectus abdominis-adductor longus (RA-AL) aponeurosis, and pubic symphysis. » There is a substantial lack of consensus on terminology and diagnostic criteria for CMI, hindering standardized evaluation, management, and research initiatives. » Diagnosis relies on structured history, physical examinations, and provocative maneuvers to identify CMI and concurrent pathology, and fluid-sensitive pelvic magnetic resonance imaging to characterize RA-AL injury. » Treatment strategies differ across sports medicine physicians, general surgeons, and orthopaedic surgeons, underscoring the need for early cross-departmental referrals to ensure all contributing pathologies are comprehensively identified and addressed. » When both adductor/RA-AL aponeurosis and inguinal canal/abdominal wall pathologies are present, prioritizing collaborative cases between orthopaedic and general surgeons is essential for decreasing operating room time, streamlining rehabilitation, and optimizing return-to-sport outcomes.

title: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy in common tendinopathies.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) was initially used for urologic issues only. After Valchanou and Michailov started applying it in orthopedics in 1991, they focused on treatment of pseudarthrosis and delayed fracture healing. Some years later, shockwave therapy was also used for tendinopathies. Today, ESWT is the first-choice treatment for tendinopathies and is unsurpassed in terms of effectivity and side effects.
METHODS: This article discusses common regions of lower extremity tendinopathies (greater trochanter pain syndrome, quadriceps tendinopathy, patellar tendinopathy, Achilles tendinopathy) in a narrative review of the evidence-based literature and guidelines of leading shockwave societies such as the International Society for Medical Shockwave Treatment (ISMST) and the Deutschsprachige internationale Gesellschaft für Extrakorporale Stosswellentherapie (DIGEST). Additional case studies are also presented.
RESULTS: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy shows excellent results in the evidence-based literature and in clinical application. No other conservative treatment option in orthopedics is described as intensively in the evidence-based literature as shockwave therapy. ESWT seems to be more effective when it is accompanied by an eccentric loading/physiotherapy program.
CONCLUSION: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy enables tendon regeneration, long-term improvement, and faster return to sport, with predictable side effects and excellent tolerance.

title: Arthroscopic Circumferential Labral Repair and Biceps Tenodesis in Elite Throwing Athletes: Technical Considerations.
abstract: SLAP lesions are a common cause of shoulder pain in overhead athletes and are often seen together with circumferential labral tearing, partial-thickness rotator cuff tearing, and biceps pathology. Isolated repair of the superior labrum has produced inconsistent outcomes, with low return-to-play rates in professional throwers. In patients with these complex cases, instability and anterior shoulder pain often coexist, and isolated labral repair or tenodesis may not be adequate treatment. Conversely, tenodesis without superior labral repair may increase glenohumeral translation. The senior author believes long head of the biceps tendon release reduces traction on the SLAP repair and may support healing. We describe an arthroscopic technique for circumferential labral repair, with knotless all-suture anchors performed in the beach-chair position, combined with open subpectoral biceps tenodesis and adjunct subacromial decompression. This technique restores stability, removes the biceps as a pain generator, eliminates traction on the repaired labrum, and preserves motion.

title: The combined influence of athletic identity and social support networks on rehabilitation adherence during sports injury recovery: A longitudinal investigation utilizing real-time experience sampling methods.
abstract: This study examined the interactive effects of athletic identity and social support on rehabilitation adherence across recovery phases among injured athletes using experience sampling methodology (ESM). A total of 142 competitive athletes (18-35 years) with moderate‑to‑severe sports injuries requiring 8-12 weeks of rehabilitation were recruited. Athletic identity and perceived social support were measured by validated questionnaires, and adherence was assessed via clinic attendance, home exercise records and therapist ratings. ESM assessments were delivered three times daily over 12 weeks. Mixed‑effects models revealed significant temporal variation in adherence, declining from 76.8% (early phase) to 64.2% (middle phase) and rising slightly to 69.5% (late phase). Athletic identity and social support exhibited a significant interaction. Athletes with high athletic identity and high social support showed 84.2% adherence, while high‑identity athletes with low support only reached 58.6%. Daily perceived social support positively predicted same‑day adherence, with emotional support exerting a stronger effect than instrumental support; the predictive model yielded an AUC of 0.847. Our findings indicate that adherence depends on the joint effect of athletic identity and social support. Clinicians should evaluate athletes' identity profiles and available social support to design tailored rehabilitation adherence interventions.

title: Imaging of acute sports injuries of the shoulder girdle.
abstract: Acute injuries of the shoulder girdle commonly result from sports activities and lead to imaging studies. Radiologists who interpret these studies should be familiar with traumatic mechanisms and the imaging manifestations of glenohumeral dislocation, acromioclavicular sprain, rotator cuff tear, labral tear, osseous contusion or fracture, and myotendinous strain. Imaging findings are crucial for making accurate diagnoses, grading the severity of injuries, guiding treatment plans, and managing the athletes' expectations for rehabilitation and return to sport. In this review article, we address common and uncommon injuries in both young and mature athletes. Focusing on magnetic resonance imaging, we provide examples of classic injuries and discuss pitfalls that challenge diagnostic interpretation.

title: Pes Anserine Bursitis: An Underrecognized Cause of Medial Knee Pain - A Review of Diagnosis, Associated Conditions, and Evidence-Based Management.
abstract: Pes anserine bursitis (PAB) is a frequently underrecognized and misdiagnosed cause of medial knee pain. It occurs when there is inflammation of the bursa interposed between the conjoined pes anserine tendons and the underlying proximal tibia. The purpose of this review is to describe the current knowledge regarding the diagnosis and management of PAB by providing an evidence-based overview of clinical exams and treatment modalities. PAB is prevalent across several high-risk populations, including knee osteoarthritis (OA), obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and athletes engaged in repetitive knee flexion activities. Diagnosis is currently limited by the absence of a validated quantitative clinical assessment tool. The main goal of treatment is to reduce associated bursal inflammation and address the underlying biomechanical and systemic contributing factors. The standard of care is conservative intervention, comprising rest, ice, and short-term NSAID use, then physical therapy and, where symptoms persist, intrabursal corticosteroid injection, with response commonly assessed at eight weeks. Surgery is considered only after these measures have been exhausted. Due to the complexity of overlapping medial knee pathology and the absence of a gold-standard diagnostic method, PAB remains a clinical diagnosis that requires thoughtful history-taking, physical examination, and selective use of imaging. This review summarizes essential clinical examination techniques and treatment options for PAB, emphasizing practical recommendations for orthopedic surgeons. The intended audience also includes sports medicine physicians, rehabilitation specialists, and primary care providers, as most cases are managed conservatively. Referral to orthopedic surgery is appropriate only when symptoms persist despite comprehensive conservative therapy. Although PAB is often diagnosed clinically, structural bursitis is confirmed in only a minority of cases, so management relies primarily on clinical assessment rather than imaging findings.

title: Optimizing Clinical Assessment of Knee Function: Biomechanical Adaptations Across Repeated Single-Leg Hop Trials.
abstract: Single-leg hop performance is widely used in clinics to assess knee function following anterior cruciate ligament injury. However, performance provides limited insight into joint-specific kinetic contributions, and the influence of repeated trials remains unclear. This study quantified the effects of hop directions (forward/vertical/backward) and repeated practice trials on performance and lower-limb joint kinetics. Forty-five injury-free participants performed 10 trials per task. Hop performance and peak moment/power/work at the hip/knee/ankle were calculated. Trials were grouped as one practice attempt and 3 blocks: I (trials 2-4), II (trials 5-7), and III (trials 8-10). Three-by-three repeated-measures analyses of variance were conducted to quantify the effects of task and practice. Backward hop demonstrated the greatest knee moment/work/power and contribution across blocks. Performance increased across blocks in forward and backward hops while remaining consistent in the vertical hop. Knee work was smaller in block I across tasks, whereas backward hop demonstrated greater knee work contribution in block II than in block I. The backward hop places greater knee emphasis, supporting its use as a knee-specific assessment. Minimal practice trials are necessary when using forward/vertical/backward hop performance to assess knee power, whereas at least 4 trials may be required for forward and vertical hops when evaluating knee work.

title: Advanced Footwear Technology in Distance Running: What We Know, What We Don't Know, and Future Directions.
abstract: Over the past decade, running shoes have undergone substantial innovation with the emergence of Advanced Footwear Technology (AFT). Shoes with AFT are typically characterized by highly compliant (deformable) and resilient (high energy return) midsole foams, embedded curved stiffening elements, low mass, and a rockered longitudinal geometry. This expert statement aims to synthesize established knowledge, remaining uncertainties and key directions for future research on AFT in middle- and long-distance running. Current literature demonstrates robust improvements in running economy and performance with AFT, with reported metabolic savings of approximately 2%-4%, and corresponding performance improvements of 1%-3%. These benefits likely arise from a combination of "acute" and possibly "long-term" mechanisms. Proposed acute mechanisms include decreased muscle force production due to higher positive work from energy-returning foams, lower muscle force production to accommodate mechanical running demands due to compliant midsoles, and improved mechanical efficiency associated with greater longitudinal bending stiffness and curved geometry. Importantly, AFT features have a synergistic effect, with the relative importance of each mechanism differing depending on the context. Emerging evidence also suggests potential reductions in muscle damage/inflammation and soreness, which could support better physiological resilience, and higher training volumes/quality. From a biomechanical injury risk perspective, AFT can redistribute loading, potentially increasing metatarsal and tarsal stress while reducing tibia and possibly Achilles tendon loading. However, injury risk associated with AFT use remains equivocal, with limited high-quality data. Notably, substantial inter-individual variability has been observed, influencing both running economy and potential injury risk although the determinants of this variability remain unclear.
